At high altitudes the ground is often frozen all year round. This **permafrost** acts like a cement that holds rock and debris together. Through **climate change** it thaws, and the slopes become less stable. The forest is also important: the **tree roots** hold the soil in place. When forests on slopes are cut down, the risk of landslides rises. That is why there are many protected **protection forests** in Switzerland.

gewusst: After the Goldau rockslide, the Goldau Nature and Animal Park was later created in the field of rubble.
About half of the forests in Switzerland protect villages, roads or railway lines from natural hazards.

teile.einleitung: The **Escadaria Selarón** is a famous staircase in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It is covered with thousands of colourful tiles and is among the most popular photo subjects in the city.
wichtigste: The Escadaria Selarón is a staircase covered with colourful tiles in Rio de Janeiro.
It was designed by the artist Jorge Selarón, who came from Chile.
He began it in the 1990s and worked on it for decades.
The tiles come from many different countries of the world.
The staircase links the districts of Lapa and Santa Teresa.

abschnitte.titel: A work of art to walk on
abschnitte.text: The staircase has over 200 steps and links the districts of **Lapa** and **Santa Teresa**. Steps and walls are covered with bright **tiles** in red, yellow, green and blue. Green, yellow and blue are the colours of Brazil’s flag. Today the staircase is a landmark of Rio and is photographed by visitors from all over the world.

**Jorge Selarón** came from Chile and lived in a house beside this staircase. At the beginning of the 1990s he began to decorate the old steps in front of his house with pieces of tile. What began as a small project became his life’s work. He described the staircase as a work that is never finished and again and again replaced tiles with new ones. Selarón died in 2013 on the staircase.

abschnitte.titel: Tiles from all over the world
abschnitte.text: At first Selarón collected tiles in the city, and later people from many countries sent him tiles. So today on the staircase there are tiles from very many countries, with pictures, coats of arms and sayings. Some of the tiles he painted himself. Anyone who looks closely keeps discovering new details on the staircase.

gewusst: The staircase appeared in music videos and adverts and became world famous as a result.

teile.einleitung: GPS is a system of satellites with which you can find your own position almost anywhere on Earth. It is built into mobile phones, cars, watches and aeroplanes.
wichtigste: GPS stands for Global Positioning System.
GPS is run by the USA.
The GPS satellites orbit at a height of about 20,000 kilometres and carry atomic clocks on board.
A receiver measures how long the radio signals take and works out the distance from that.
To get a position including height, at least 4 satellites are needed.
Other systems are Galileo from Europe and GLONASS from Russia.

abschnitte.text: **GPS** is short for **Global Positioning System**. It was originally developed for the military by the **USA** and is still run by them today. Around the Earth orbit about 30 satellites at a height of about **20,000 kilometres**. They are spread out so that almost anywhere on Earth you can receive several of them at the same time.

Every satellite constantly sends out a **radio signal** with the exact time and its position. A GPS receiver, for example in a mobile phone, picks up these signals. From the **travel time of the signal** it works out how far it is from the satellite. Because radio waves travel at the speed of light, extremely accurate clocks are needed for this. That is why the satellites carry **atomic clocks** on board.

With the distances to several satellites, the receiver can work out its location. Three satellites would be enough for position and height if the receiver itself had a perfect clock. But the clock in a mobile phone is not accurate. So at least **4 satellites** are needed: this way the receiver can determine its position including height and the exact time at once.

Besides GPS there are other satellite navigation systems. Europe runs **Galileo**, Russia has **GLONASS** and China has the system **BeiDou**. Modern mobile phones often use several systems at once and become more accurate as a result. In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Topography swisstopo runs fixed reference stations. With these, surveys can become accurate to within a few centimetres.

GPS helps drivers, hikers, ships and aeroplanes to find their way. Farmers also use it to steer tractors very precisely across their fields. A popular leisure activity is **geocaching**: using coordinates, you look for small hidden containers. Inside there is often a logbook in which you write your name. Many such hiding places can be found in Switzerland too.

gewusst: Without corrections based on Albert Einstein’s theory of relativity, GPS positions would be wrong by kilometres after just one day.
GPS has been fully in operation since the mid-1990s.

teile.einleitung: The Darién Gap is a stretch of jungle on the border between Panama and Colombia. There the Pan-American Highway, the long road through the Americas, is broken. To this day no road runs through this area.
wichtigste: The Darién Gap lies between Panama and Colombia.
The Pan-American Highway is broken here.
The area is covered with dense rainforest, swamps and mountains.
A large part of it is protected as a national park.
Vehicles are carried around the gap by ship.

abschnitte.text: The **Pan-American Highway** is a road network that stretches from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego in the south of South America. There is only one place where there is no road: in the **Darién**, on the border between **Panama** and **Colombia**. The gap is about 100 kilometres long. Anyone who wants to drive through the whole of the Americas has to take their vehicle on by **ship** here.

In the Darién there is dense **rainforest**, large **swamps**, rivers and mountains. It rains a great deal. Building a road would be difficult and expensive. Many people also deliberately want to keep the gap in order to protect the forest, the animals and the indigenous peoples who live there. **Darién National Park** in Panama is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Although there is no road, many people cross the Darién on foot every year. They are often **migrants** on their way north. The journey takes several days and is very dangerous because of rivers, heat, disease and crime. Aid organisations look after people who come out of the jungle.

gewusst: The Pan-American Highway is one of the longest road networks in the world, but a stretch is missing right in the middle.
The Darién is one of the wettest and most species-rich areas in the Americas.

teile.einleitung: In Antarctica there are no cities, but there are many research stations. There, experts from all over the world study the ice, the weather, the animals and the climate of the Earth.
wichtigste: The largest station in Antarctica is the American McMurdo Station.
Beneath the Russian Vostok Station lies the great Lake Vostok.
Germany runs the Neumayer Station III.
France and Italy jointly run the Concordia Station.
The Belgian Princess Elisabeth Station works with no CO2 emissions.
The Swiss Polar Institute has supported Swiss polar research since 2016.

abschnitte.text: Antarctica belongs to no single country. The **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959 lays down that the continent is used only peacefully, above all for **research**. Many countries run stations there. Some are staffed only in summer, others all year round. In winter it is dark and extremely cold there for months.

The largest station is the **McMurdo Station** of the USA on Ross Island. In summer over 1,000 people live there. The Russian **Vostok Station** lies high up on the ice. About 4 kilometres below it lies **Lake Vostok**, the largest known lake under the Antarctic ice. At Vostok, the lowest air temperature ever measured on Earth was recorded in 1983.

The **Neumayer Station III** is run by the German **Alfred Wegener Institute**. It stands on stilts on the Ekström Ice Shelf. The British station **Halley VI** stands on the Brunt Ice Shelf, which is constantly moving. Its modules therefore have legs with **skis** and were towed to another site in 2017.

The **Concordia Station** stands high on the ice plateau at Dome C. It is run jointly by **France and Italy**. The Belgian station **Princess Elisabeth** was opened in 2009. It gets its energy from **wind and sun** and is regarded as the first station in Antarctica with no CO2 emissions in operation.

Switzerland has no station of its own in Antarctica. Swiss researchers often take part in projects of other countries, though. In 2016 the **Swiss Polar Institute** was founded. It supports research in the **Arctic, Antarctica and high mountains**. It also organised an expedition with a ship around Antarctica.

gewusst: The ice of Antarctica is over 4 kilometres thick in some places.
From deep ice cores, researchers can read off what the climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: Frost wedging is a kind of weathering. Water gets into cracks in the rock, freezes and expands as it does so. In this way the rock is gradually forced apart.
wichtigste: Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes.
Frost wedging works most strongly when frost and thaw alternate often.
In the Alps it is especially strong above the tree line.
At the foot of rock faces, scree slopes form in this way.
Rock with many fissures and porous rock is especially vulnerable.
Potholes in roads form on the same principle.

abschnitte.text: Most substances contract when they cool. Water is an exception: ice has a **lower density** than liquid water. When it freezes, water expands by about **9 per cent**. If it is trapped in a crack in the rock, the ice presses against the walls with great force. In this way the crack is widened bit by bit.

What matters is many **freeze-thaw cycles**. When it thaws, water gets deeper into the cracks. At the next freeze it forces them open further. Permanent frost alone has a much weaker effect. **Rock with many fissures and porous rock** is especially vulnerable, because it takes up a lot of water.

In the Alps, frost wedging is especially strong **above the tree line**. There, freeze-thaw cycles are frequent and there are hardly any protective plants. Stones that are split off fall down the face and collect at the foot of the slope as **scree slopes**. In **spring**, during the snowmelt, frost and thaw often alternate. Then **rockfall** happens more often.

Besides high mountains, the **subpolar tundra** is typical for strong frost wedging. There too there are many freeze-thaw cycles and hardly any protective vegetation. Frost debris shapes large parts of the landscape there. In warm regions without frost, by contrast, this kind of weathering does not occur.

Damage to roads arises on the same principle. Water gets into small cracks in the surface, freezes and expands. After several freeze-thaw cycles, the surface breaks up. This is how **frost heaves** and **potholes** form. After a winter with many freeze-thaw cycles, road workers therefore have a lot to do.

gewusst: Ice floats on water because it is lighter than the same amount of liquid water.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst for the same reason.

teile.einleitung: **Fishing** is the catching or farming of fish and other water animals. It provides food and work for millions of people in the world, but it is also a danger to fish stocks if too much is caught.
wichtigste: China catches and farms the most fish (as of 2024).
At sea, fishermen catch many fish at once with a **net**.
A smaller fishing boat on the coast is called a **cutter**.
In angling, you put a **bait** on the hook.
When fish are raised in tanks, this is called **fish farming**.
Norway supplies especially much farmed salmon.

abschnitte.text: At sea, fishermen catch many fish at once with a large **net**. On the coast they are often out in a smaller fishing boat called a **cutter**. Far out on the ocean, by contrast, huge factory ships work, which process the catch on board. In **angling** with a rod, you put a **bait**, for example a worm, on the hook to attract the fish.

Today a large share of fish is no longer caught wild but farmed. When fish are raised in tanks or net pens, this is called **fish farming** or **aquaculture**. Especially much **farmed salmon** comes from **Norway**, where the salmon swim in large pens in the fjords. Worldwide, **China** catches and farms the most fish (as of 2024).

When more fish are caught than can grow back, this is called **overfishing**. Many stocks in the sea have therefore shrunk strongly. One example is **tuna**, a large sea fish that often comes into the shop in tins. To protect the fish there are **catch quotas**, protected areas and rules for the size of net meshes. Labels on the packaging show whether a fish was caught or farmed sustainably.

In Switzerland, professional fishermen fish mainly in the large lakes. The most important fish is the **whitefish**, and also perch and Arctic char. Many people fish in their free time. For this you usually need a **fishing licence**, which the canton issues. Anyone who wants a licence often has to attend a course first, in which they learn how to treat fish gently.

gewusst: Most of the fish eaten in Switzerland comes from abroad.
A tuna can swim very fast and covers huge distances on its migrations.

teile.einleitung: A chokepoint in shipping is a narrow strait or a canal through which very many ships have to pass. If traffic is disrupted there, the whole world feels it.
wichtigste: A **chokepoint** is a bottleneck that can hardly be bypassed.
Important chokepoints include the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal and the Panama Canal.
About a fifth of the oil consumed worldwide flows through the **Strait of Hormuz**.
In 2023 the Panama Canal had to restrict passages because of a drought.
The **Montreux Convention** of 1936 regulates passage through the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles.
At its narrowest point the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide.

abschnitte.text: Most of world trade is carried by **ships**. Many routes lead through narrow places between two land masses or through artificial canals. When such a place is blocked, ships have to make huge detours or wait. Goods then arrive later, and prices can rise. Even Switzerland, with no coast, depends on this, because many goods reach it through seaports and then up the Rhine as far as **Basel**.

The **Strait of Hormuz** links the Persian Gulf with the open sea. Tankers with oil from several Gulf states pass through here. According to the US Energy Information Administration, about a **fifth** of the oil consumed worldwide passes through this strait. There are only a few pipelines that bypass it, which is why it is especially sensitive.

The **Suez Canal** in Egypt links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. In 2021 the huge container ship “Ever Given” got stuck there and blocked the canal for almost a week. The **Panama Canal** lifts ships over land with locks. The water for this comes from **Gatún Lake**. When a drought lowered the water level in 2023, the draught and the number of passages were restricted.

Anyone who wants to get from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean has to pass through the **Bosphorus** at Istanbul and the **Dardanelles**. Since 1936 the **Montreux Convention** has regulated this passage. It was signed in Switzerland on Lake Geneva. Merchant ships may pass freely, Turkey controls the straits, and restrictions apply to warships.

At its narrowest point, the **Strait of Gibraltar** between Spain and Morocco is only about 14 km wide. All the shipping between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic passes through it. In the north, the **Danish straits** of the Øresund and the Great and Little Belt link the Baltic with the North Sea, unless you take the Kiel Canal. In Asia the **Strait of Malacca** is one of the busiest sea routes in the world.

gewusst: A single stuck ship in the Suez Canal held up hundreds of other ships in 2021.
The Panama Canal needs large amounts of fresh water for every passage of a ship, so it is drought that can be dangerous to it.

teile.einleitung: **Ferdinand Magellan** was a Portuguese seafarer. His expedition achieved the first voyage round the world from 1519 to 1522, even though he himself did not live to see the return.
wichtigste: Magellan’s expedition is famous for the first circumnavigation of the world.
Born in Portugal, he sailed on behalf of **Spain**.
In 1519 the fleet set off with five ships.
Magellan named the great ocean the **Pacific**, the peaceful ocean.
He died in 1521 in the Philippines.
Only the ship **Victoria** returned to Spain in 1522, with 18 men.

abschnitte.titel: A Portuguese in the service of Spain
abschnitte.text: Ferdinand Magellan was born in **Portugal** and went to sea while still young. He wanted to reach the Spice Islands in Asia by sailing west. The Portuguese king did not support his plan. Magellan therefore went to **Spain**, where the young King Charles gave him ships. Spices such as cloves and nutmeg were very valuable at that time.

In 1519 the fleet set off from Spain with **five ships**. It crossed the Atlantic and sailed south along the coast of South America. There Magellan looked for a passage to the other sea. In 1520 he found a dangerous strait, which is now called the **Strait of Magellan**. Afterwards he reached a huge, calm ocean and named it the **Pacific**, the peaceful ocean.

The voyage across the Pacific took much longer than expected. The men suffered from hunger and disease. Finally the fleet reached the **Philippines**. There in 1521 Magellan got into a fight with residents of the island of Mactan and lost his life. The remaining sailors continued the voyage without him.

Of the five ships, only the **Victoria** completed the voyage. Under the command of **Juan Sebastián Elcano** she returned to Spain in 1522. On board there were only **18 men** left. They had been the first people to sail round the Earth. The voyage proved that you can sail round the whole world and that the Earth is much bigger than many people then thought.

gewusst: The **Magellanic Clouds** are two galaxies in the southern sky that are named after him.
The sailors who came home found that a day was missing from their calendar, because they had travelled west with the Sun.

teile.einleitung: The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco is one of the most famous bridges in the world. Since 1937 the orange-red suspension bridge has spanned the strait between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific.
wichtigste: The Golden Gate Bridge stands in San Francisco in the US state of California.
It was opened in 1937.
It is a suspension bridge with 2 tall towers.
It is about 2.7 kilometres long.
Its colour is orange-red.
It is often almost completely hidden by fog.

abschnitte.text: The **Golden Gate Bridge** is a **suspension bridge**. This means that the roadway hangs from thick steel cables that are strung over **two tall towers**. At both ends the cables are firmly anchored in the ground. The bridge is about **2.7 kilometres** long in all. The towers rise over 200 metres above the water. When it was opened, it had the longest span of any suspension bridge in the world.

The bridge crosses a **strait** called the **Golden Gate**. It connects San Francisco Bay with the **Pacific Ocean**. The bridge leads from the city of San Francisco north to Marin County in **California**. Because there are strong currents and wind there, building it was difficult. After several years of construction it was opened in **1937**.

The bridge is not golden, but **orange-red**. The colour is called “International Orange”. It was chosen because it suits the landscape well and is easy to see even in fog. To stop the steel from rusting, the bridge is constantly maintained and repainted. Across the bridge there is a road as well as paths for pedestrians and cyclists.

San Francisco is known for its thick **fog**, which rolls in from the sea. Especially in summer it often hides the bridge almost completely, and only the tops of the towers peek out. In the bay nearby lies the small island of **Alcatraz**. A famous prison used to stand there, and today the island is a museum that you can visit by boat.

gewusst: The main span between the two towers is about 1.3 kilometres long.
The Golden Gate Bridge is one of the most photographed structures in the world.

teile.einleitung: A **fjord** is a long, narrow and deep inlet of the sea that reaches far inland. Fjords were formed by glaciers in the Ice Age and are especially typical of Norway.
wichtigste: A fjord is a glacially deepened trough valley that was flooded by the sea.
At the mouth there is often a **sill** of rock or moraine, so it is less deep there.
The Sognefjord is the longest and deepest fjord in Norway.
The Geirangerfjord and the Nærøyfjord have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2005.
Most fjord coasts lie in middle and high latitudes of both hemispheres.
A **firth** (Förde) like the one at Kiel is shallower and has gentle shores.

abschnitte.text: In the **Ice Age**, mighty glaciers flowed from the mountains to the sea. They carved out deep valleys with steep walls, called **trough valleys**. The glaciers even dug the valleys deeper than sea level, which experts call **overdeepened**. When the ice melted, the sea rose and flooded the valleys. This is how the fjords formed. At the exit a fjord is often less deep, because there lies a **sill** of rock or moraine.

Norway is the best-known country of fjords. The **Sognefjord** is the longest and deepest fjord in the country. It reaches over 200 kilometres inland and is over 1,000 metres deep in places. Especially beautiful are the **Geirangerfjord** and the **Nærøyfjord** with waterfalls and steep rock walls. In 2005 they were jointly added to the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

Fjords exist where glaciers reached the sea in the Ice Age. Most fjord coasts therefore lie in **middle and high latitudes** of both hemispheres. Examples are Norway, Canada, Alaska, Chile and New Zealand. In **Greenland** lies **Scoresby Sund**, one of the largest fjord systems in the world. A **firth** like the one at Kiel on the Baltic is, by contrast, shallower and fringed by gentle shores.

The sill at the exit hinders the **exchange of water** with the open sea. As a result the **deep water** in some fjords is poor in oxygen. A danger is **rockfalls** from the steep walls. In 1958 in **Lituya Bay** in Alaska, an earthquake set off a rockfall. The flood wave ran over 500 metres up the opposite slope, higher than any wave ever measured.

gewusst: The word “fjord” comes from Norwegian and is related to the English word “ford”.
Large cruise ships can sail deep into some Norwegian fjords because they are so deep.

teile.einleitung: Death Valley is a desert valley in the west of the USA. It is one of the hottest and driest places on Earth. The lowest point in North America is also here.
wichtigste: Most of Death Valley lies in California, and a small part in Nevada.
It belongs to the Mojave Desert.
Badwater Basin lies 86 metres below sea level.
In 1913, 56.7 °C was measured here.
It is so hot and dry because it lies low and in the rain shadow of high mountain ranges.
On the Racetrack Playa, stones move across the ground.

abschnitte.text: Death Valley lies mostly in **California** and extends into Nevada. It belongs to the **Mojave Desert**. It got its name during the gold rush around 1849, when settlers on their way west crossed the valley only with great difficulty. Today it is a **national park**, the largest in the USA outside Alaska.

**Badwater Basin** lies **86 metres below sea level** and is the lowest point in North America. The ground there is covered with a white **crust of salt**. It forms because water evaporates and the salt is left behind. Only about 140 kilometres away stands Mount Whitney, one of the highest mountains in the USA.

On 10 July **1913**, **56.7 °C** was measured in Death Valley. This is regarded as the highest air temperature ever measured in the world. It is so hot because the valley lies **low** and is surrounded by mountains. The warm air can hardly escape. It also lies in the **rain shadow** of high mountain ranges: the clouds lose their rain over the mountains first.

On the **Racetrack Playa**, a dried-up lake bed, there are stones with long tracks behind them. For a long time it was a mystery how they moved. In 2014, researchers found the answer: in winter, a thin layer of water forms after rain and freezes at night. **Thin sheets of ice** are then pushed by the **wind** and carry the stones along.

gewusst: In Death Valley, the lowest point in North America and one of the highest mountains in the USA are only about 140 kilometres apart.
Despite the heat and dryness, animals such as coyotes, lizards and tiny fish in salt springs live in Death Valley.

teile.einleitung: Dharavi is a huge residential and commercial district in the middle of Mumbai, the largest city in India. It is regarded as one of the largest informal settlements in Asia. In a very small space, an enormous number of people live and work.
wichtigste: Dharavi lies in the centre of Mumbai, which used to be called Bombay.
Its area is only about 2 square kilometres.
Estimates range from several hundred thousand to about a million residents.
Originally there was a marshland here with a fishing village of the Koli.
In thousands of small workshops, mainly waste is recycled.
The film “Slumdog Millionaire” made Dharavi known worldwide.
In 2022 the Adani Group received the contract to redevelop the district.

abschnitte.titel: From fishing village to city district
abschnitte.text: Where Dharavi lies today, there used to be swamps and **mangroves**. The **Koli**, a community of fishermen, lived there. As Bombay grew, more and more people from all over India moved to the city. Many could not find an affordable home and built themselves simple huts in Dharavi. In this way a densely built district with narrow lanes gradually came into being.

Dharavi is not only a place to live but also a large **commercial area**. **Recycling** is especially well known: plastic, metal, paper and other waste are collected, sorted and reused. Small businesses also make leather goods, clothes and food. Many products are sold all over India and even abroad. Together, the workshops earn a great deal of money.

A special part of Dharavi is called **Kumbharwada**. Potter families live there whose ancestors once came from the state of **Gujarat**. The name comes from the word “kumbhar”, which means potter. The families shape clay vessels and fire them in traditional kilns. The finished pots often stand in the lanes to dry.

abschnitte.titel: Living and working in very little space
abschnitte.text: Typical of Dharavi is the **mixing of uses**: living and working take place in the same spot. A room serves as a workshop by day and as a place to sleep at night. The houses stand very close together, and there is little green space. Clean water, toilets and sewers are missing in many places. Even so, people stick closely together and have built a lively neighbourhood.

Dharavi lies very centrally between two important **suburban railway lines** and close to the modern business district of **Bandra Kurla Complex**. This makes the land extremely valuable. For years there have been plans to tear the district down and rebuild it. In 2022 the government of the state of Maharashtra awarded the large project to the **Adani Group**. Supporters hope for better homes, while critics fear that residents and small businesses will be pushed out.

gewusst: Parts of the film “Slumdog Millionaire”, which won the Oscar for best picture in 2009, were shot in Dharavi.
Dharavi is smaller than many Swiss municipalities but is among the most densely populated places in the world.
Guided tours are offered in Dharavi, and they are argued over: some see real interest in them, others see disrespect.

teile.einleitung: Geothermal energy means heat from the interior of the Earth. The deeper you drill, the warmer it gets. This heat can be used for heating and, in some places, also for generating electricity.
wichtigste: Geothermal energy is the use of the Earth’s heat.
In the Earth’s crust, it gets about 3 degrees warmer on average for every 100 metres of depth.
Iceland heats most of its houses with geothermal heat.
In Switzerland many houses are heated with ground source heat probes and heat pumps.
Geothermal heat is independent of the weather and almost always available.

abschnitte.text: In the interior of the Earth it is very hot. Part of this heat still dates from the formation of the Earth, and another part is produced by the decay of natural **radioactive substances** in the rock. In the Earth’s crust the temperature rises on average by about **3 degrees** for every 100 metres of depth. In places with **volcanoes**, hot rock lies much closer to the surface. There, geothermal energy is especially easy to use.

**Iceland** lies on a very volcanically active area. There most houses are heated with **geothermal heat**. Hot water from the depths flows through pipes into homes and even under pavements so that no ice forms there. Iceland also generates part of its electricity in geothermal power stations. The country’s famous warm bathing lagoons are also heated by geothermal heat.

In Switzerland there are no volcanoes, yet geothermal heat is widespread. Many houses have a **ground source heat probe**: a pipe that reaches a few hundred metres down into the ground. A **heat pump** draws the heat from the ground with it and heats the house. Switzerland is among the countries with an especially large number of such probes. For electricity, though, you would need very deep boreholes, which is difficult. In **Basel** such a project was stopped in 2006 after noticeable earthquakes.

Geothermal heat has great advantages: it is available almost without limit, causes few exhaust gases in operation and supplies energy independently of the weather, day and night. However, deep boreholes are expensive, and you do not always know exactly beforehand how hot the rock is. In addition, boreholes at great depth can trigger small earthquakes. The technology is therefore carefully researched.

gewusst: In 1904, electricity was generated from geothermal heat for the first time in Larderello in Italy.

teile.einleitung: Diamond is the hardest natural substance in the world. When cut, it sparkles like hardly any other stone and is therefore regarded as an especially valuable gemstone. Yet it consists of a quite ordinary element: carbon.
wichtigste: Diamond is the hardest natural substance.
A diamond consists of pure carbon.
Diamonds form deep in the Earth under great pressure and great heat.
Only cutting makes a diamond begin to sparkle.
A round diamond cut with many faces is called a brilliant.
The weight of diamonds is measured in carats.
Botswana in Africa is among the most important diamond countries.

abschnitte.text: A diamond consists of **carbon**, the same element as the lead of a pencil (graphite). The difference lies in how the tiny particles are arranged. In a diamond, the carbon atoms are joined in a very firm, regular lattice. That is why it is so hard. On the **Mohs** scale of hardness it has the highest value, namely 10.

Diamonds form **deep in the Earth’s mantle**, well over 100 kilometres below the surface. There, enormous pressure and great heat prevail. Many diamonds are hundreds of millions or even billions of years old. They reach the surface with magma that rises in narrow volcanic pipes. The rock in these pipes is called **kimberlite**, named after the town of Kimberley in South Africa.

A freshly found rough diamond looks rather plain. Only the **cut** makes it sparkle. Many small, smooth surfaces called **facets** are added. They steer the light so that it is thrown back and forth inside the stone and split into the colours of the rainbow. The best-known cut is the **brilliant**: round, with 57 or 58 facets. Because only diamond can scratch diamond, it is cut with diamond powder.

The weight of gemstones is measured in **carats**. One carat equals 0.2 grams. For the value of a diamond, colour, clarity and the quality of the cut count as well as weight. Diamonds are often made into jewellery, such as an **engagement ring**. Many diamonds that are found, however, are too small or too impure for this and are used in industry.

Important producing countries are **Botswana**, Russia, Canada, South Africa and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Botswana, diamond mining contributed greatly to the country’s prosperity. In industry, diamonds serve as the tips of drills and as the coating of saws that cut stone or concrete. Today diamonds can also be made artificially in factories.

gewusst: The largest rough diamond ever found is the “Cullinan” from South Africa: it weighed over 3,000 carats, that is, more than 600 grams.
The name diamond comes from the Greek word “adamas”, which means “unconquerable”.
Although diamond is so hard, it can burn at very high temperatures, because it consists of carbon.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake the ground trembles and shakes. This happens when parts of the Earth’s crust suddenly shift. The Earth also quakes in Switzerland, but usually only weakly.
wichtigste: Earthquakes arise when **tectonic plates** shift with a jerk.
Most earthquakes occur at the **boundaries of the plates**.
The point on the surface above the focus is called the **epicentre**.
After a big quake, **aftershocks** often follow.
Earthquake waves are recorded with a **seismograph**.
In Switzerland, quakes are most frequent in the **Valais**.
In 1356 **Basel** was destroyed by a strong earthquake.

abschnitte.text: The Earth’s crust consists of large **plates** that lie against each other like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. They move very slowly, only a few centimetres a year. At their **boundaries** they catch on each other, and tension builds up. When the rock suddenly gives way, the tension is released with a jerk, and the Earth quakes. That is why most earthquakes occur where plates meet.

An earthquake begins deep in the Earth at the **earthquake focus**. The point directly above it on the surface is called the **epicentre**. There the quake is usually felt most strongly. After a strong quake the Earth often shakes several more times. These weaker tremors are called **aftershocks**.

With a **seismograph** the movements of the ground are measured. The record, a jagged line, is called a **seismogram**. In Switzerland the **Swiss Seismological Service** monitors all earthquakes. It belongs to **ETH Zurich**, runs many measuring stations across the country and assesses where earthquakes could become especially dangerous.

Switzerland does not lie on a large plate boundary, yet many small quakes are measured every year. Quakes are most frequent in the **Valais**, which is connected with the formation of the Alps. The **Basel** region is also at risk: in 1356 an earthquake destroyed large parts of the city, and many houses collapsed or burned. It was one of the strongest quakes in Central Europe.

In an earthquake inside a house, it is best to go **under a sturdy table** and hold on to a table leg. In this way you are protected from falling objects. Stay away from windows, because glass can break. Do not use the **lift**, because it can get stuck. When the quake is over, you calmly go outside, away from buildings.

gewusst: In Switzerland only a few earthquakes are felt each year, but hundreds are measured that are too weak for people to notice.
The Basel earthquake of 1356 was so strong that it was felt far beyond the region.

teile.einleitung: On many coasts the sea level rises and falls regularly. This change between low tide and high tide is called the tides. It is caused mainly by the Moon.
wichtigste: Low tide and high tide together are called the tides.
The tides are mainly caused by the Moon.
It takes about 6 hours from low tide to high tide.
On most coasts the high tide comes roughly twice a day.
A tide table tells you when the low and high tides are.
The Wadden Sea on the North Sea dries out at low tide.

abschnitte.text: When the water at the sea goes back and the water level falls, this is called **low tide** (or **ebb**). When the water rises again, it is **high tide** (or **flood**). Both together are called the **tides**. It takes about **6 hours** from low tide to high tide. On most coasts there are therefore roughly **two high tides a day** and two low tides, each day a little later than the day before.

With its **gravity**, the **Moon** pulls on the water of the Earth. On the side facing the Moon, a bulge of water forms. A bulge of water also forms on the opposite side of the Earth. As the Earth turns, every coastal place moves through these bulges of water, and that is how the high tide comes about. The **Sun** also plays a part: when the Sun and the Moon are in a line, the tides are especially strong.

On the **North Sea** off Germany, the Netherlands and Denmark lies the **Wadden Sea**. At low tide a huge strip of seabed dries out there. In the mud live worms, mussels and crabs, which many birds feed on. The Wadden Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At low tide you can go on a **mudflat walk** with a guide.

Because the tides are regular, they can be worked out in advance. A **tide table** says when low tide and high tide are at a particular place. This is very important for fishermen, ships and mudflat walkers. Anyone who underestimates the high tide can be caught out by the rising water on the mudflats. That is why you should never go out without knowing the times.

In Swiss lakes there are hardly any tides. The reason: the **lakes are too small**. For the Moon to create a noticeable bulge of water, you need a very large body of water such as an ocean. On Lake Geneva or Lake Constance the effect is tiny and cannot be noticed in everyday life. Water levels in lakes here change mainly because of rain and melting snow.

gewusst: In the Bay of Fundy in Canada the water rises by up to about 15 metres at high tide, which is one of the biggest tidal differences in the world.
The solid crust of the Earth also rises and falls a little because of the Moon’s pull, but you cannot notice it.

teile.einleitung: The zebra mussel is a small freshwater mussel with a three-edged shell and a zigzag pattern. Because of these stripes it is called the zebra mussel. It originally comes from Eastern Europe, and today it lives in many lakes and rivers worldwide.
wichtigste: The zebra mussel was originally called the three-edged mussel (Dreikantmuschel) in German.
It comes originally from the area around the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
It usually grows only 2 to 4 centimetres.
From the end of the 1980s, it spread explosively in the Great Lakes of North America.
It attaches itself with fine threads to stones, boats and pipes.

abschnitte.text: The **zebra mussel** is only about as big as a fingernail up to the length of a thumb joint. Its shell has three edges and a light and dark **zigzag pattern**, which is why it is called the **zebra mussel**. With fine, strong threads, the **byssus threads**, it sticks itself to hard surfaces. Often thousands sit close together. It filters water and in the process eats tiny algae and floating particles.

Originally the mussel lived in the area around the **Black Sea** and the **Caspian Sea**. Through canals and on ships it spread across the whole of Europe as early as the 19th century. It reached the Swiss lakes in the 20th century. From the **end of the 1980s**, it spread **explosively in the Great Lakes** of North America. Its larvae probably got there in the **ballast water** of cargo ships.

The mussels multiply very fast and clog water pipes, cooling systems and pipes in power stations. Cleaning them costs a lot of money. They also push out native mussels. At the same time they make the water clearer, and water birds such as the **tufted duck** like to eat them. In Switzerland the related **quagga mussel** is now spreading strongly, so boats should be cleaned before being moved to another lake.

gewusst: A single zebra mussel can filter about a litre of water every day.

teile.einleitung: The polar bear lives in the Arctic around the North Pole. It is one of the largest predators on land and an excellent swimmer. Its life is closely tied to the sea ice.
wichtigste: Polar bears live in the Arctic around the North Pole.
They like best to eat seals.
With their noses they smell prey from far away.
Under the white fur their skin is black.
Thick fur and a layer of fat protect them from the cold.
A female polar bear usually gives birth to two cubs in a snow den.
When the sea ice melts, hunting becomes difficult for them.

abschnitte.text: The **polar bear** lives in the **Arctic**, for example in Canada, Greenland, Alaska, Russia and on Svalbard. It is often icy cold there. A **thick coat** and a thick **layer of fat** keep it warm. Its fur looks white, but the individual hairs are actually transparent. Underneath, the **skin is black**. Male polar bears can weigh several hundred kilograms.

Polar bears like best to eat **seals**. With their fine **noses** they smell a seal from a great distance, even under the snow. They often wait patiently at a breathing hole in the ice until a seal appears. The **sea ice** is therefore like a hunting ground to them. In summer, when there is less ice, many polar bears have to get by for a long time without much food.

Polar bears can **swim very well**. With their big, broad front paws they paddle as if with oars. They can swim many kilometres from one ice floe to the next. Their fur and fat help them not to get chilled in the cold water. Their scientific name even means “sea bear”.

In winter the female polar bear digs a **snow den**. In it she gives birth to her young, usually **two**. The little ones are tiny, blind and almost naked at birth. In the warm den they grow fast. In spring they leave the den for the first time. After that they stay with their mother for about two years and learn hunting from her.

Because of **climate change**, the sea ice in the Arctic melts earlier and forms later. Because polar bears **hunt on the ice**, they then find fewer seals. Many have to go hungry for longer or swim very far. Experts fear that there will therefore be fewer polar bears in the future. The species is regarded as vulnerable.

gewusst: Together with the Kodiak bear, the polar bear is among the largest predators living on land.
The soles of polar bears’ paws are covered with fur and small bumps so that they do not slip on the ice.

teile.einleitung: A drought is a long period in which far too little rain or snow falls. Soils dry out, plants wither and rivers carry little water. Droughts can bring whole regions into hardship, and they also affect Switzerland.
wichtigste: A drought is a long period with far too little precipitation.
In the Sahel zone there were severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s.
When desert-like areas spread, this is called desertification.
In the 1930s the Dust Bowl struck the Great Plains of the USA.
In summer 2018 the Swiss Army flew water to cows on alpine pastures.
When the Rhine is low, ships can carry less.
El Niño often leads to droughts in Australia and Indonesia.

abschnitte.text: We speak of a **drought** when **far too little precipitation** falls over a long time. First the rain is missing, then the soil dries out. Later the levels of rivers and lakes fall too, and so does the **groundwater**. To spot a drought in farming early, people measure the **soil moisture**, that is, how much water is in the ground. Heat makes a drought worse, because more water then evaporates.

The **Sahel zone** on the southern edge of the Sahara suffered severe droughts in the **1970s and 1980s**. Many people lost their harvests and their livestock, and there were famines. In some areas desert-like land spread, partly because soils were overused. This is called **desertification**. The climate phenomenon **El Niño** in the Pacific often leads to droughts in **Australia** and **Indonesia**.

In the **1930s** a severe drought struck the **Great Plains** in the USA. Farmers had previously ploughed up huge areas of grassland. When the rain stayed away, the soil dried out, and the wind whirled it up in gigantic **dust storms**. This disaster is called the **Dust Bowl**. Many families had to leave their farms. Afterwards people learned to protect soils better, for example with rows of trees against the wind.

Switzerland also experiences droughts, for example in the summers of **2003** and **2018**. In the drought summer of 2018 the **Swiss Army** transported water by **helicopter** to **alpine pastures** so that the **cows** had enough to drink. Streams dried up, and fish had to be rescued. In many cantons a **ban on fires** applied in the forest, because the risk of fire was high.

A long drought lowers the water level of rivers. On the **Rhine**, cargo ships can then **load less**, because otherwise they would run aground. This makes transport more expensive, including for goods that reach Switzerland by way of Basel. Little water also means less electricity from **hydroelectric power stations**. Experts expect droughts to become more frequent with **climate change**.

gewusst: In times of great dryness, old “hunger stones” sometimes appear in rivers such as the Elbe, in which earlier generations carved the years of droughts.
A drought cannot be recognised on a single day: it develops slowly over weeks, months or even years.

teile.einleitung: Demographic change means that the make-up of a population changes, above all its age. In Switzerland and many other countries there are more and more older people and fewer young people. This has consequences for schools, work, health and the AHV old-age pension.
wichtigste: Society is ageing because few children are born and people live longer.
In Switzerland in 2024, the birth rate was about 1.3 children per woman.
Life expectancy at birth in Switzerland in 2024 was about 84 years.
An ageing, shrinking population has a population pyramid in the shape of an urn.
The old-age dependency ratio compares the number of people aged 65 and over with those of working age.
With the AHV, fewer and fewer people in work pay for more and more pensions.
Japan has one of the highest shares of people aged 65 and over.

abschnitte.text: The term **demographic change** describes changes in the size and make-up of a population. Especially important is **ageing**: the share of older people is growing. There are two main causes, a low birth rate and rising life expectancy. Immigration also changes the population.

A **population pyramid** shows how many people live at each age, men on the left and women on the right. If many children are born, it is wide at the bottom and has the shape of a real pyramid. If the numbers stay the same, it looks like a bell. If only a few children are born, it becomes narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, which is called an **urn shape**.

In Switzerland in 2024, about 1.3 children were born per woman, clearly fewer than the 2.1 children needed to keep the level steady. At the same time, **life expectancy** at birth was about 84 years, and women live slightly longer on average than men. Around 1900, life expectancy was still under 50 years. The large **baby boomer** generations from the 1950s and 1960s are now retiring.

The **old-age dependency ratio** shows how many people aged 65 and over there are for every 100 people aged 20 to 64. An example: 1.8 million older people divided by 5.4 million people of working age gives about 33. This means that for every 100 people of working age there are about 33 pensioners. If this figure rises, fewer young people have to support more older people.

The **AHV** was introduced in 1948 and works on the **pay-as-you-go principle**. This means that people in work directly pay for the pensions of today’s retired people with their contributions. If there are fewer people in work and more pensioners, this becomes harder. That is why reforms are discussed again and again in Switzerland, for example the retirement age or higher contributions.

Japan is one of the countries with the highest share of people aged 65 and over, and almost one person in three belongs to this group. Italy, Germany and South Korea are also ageing strongly. In many African countries, on the other hand, the population is very young. Ageing also brings opportunities, for example new jobs in care and active older people.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many years a newborn baby will live on average.
How many children a woman has on average.
The number of people aged 65 and over per 100 people of working age.
Those who are working today pay for the pensions of those who are retired today.

gewusst: In Switzerland today there are several thousand people who are 100 years old or older.
In 1948, when the AHV started, there were many more people in work for each pensioner than there are today.

teile.einleitung: The Three Gorges barrage is a gigantic dam wall on the Yangtze in China. It forms a very long reservoir and drives the most powerful hydroelectric power station on Earth. At the same time it is an example of how a huge structure changes landscape and life.
wichtigste: The barrage holds back the Yangtze in Hubei Province.
The dam wall is 181 metres high and was completed in 2006.
The power station has an output of about 22,500 megawatts.
About 1.3 million people had to be resettled.
The barrage also serves flood protection on the middle and lower reaches.
Two flights of locks, each with five stages, lead ships past the dam.
Because sediments are held back, mud is missing downstream.

abschnitte.text: The barrage stands on the **Yangtze** in **Hubei** Province. It is a concrete **gravity dam**: its own enormous weight withstands the pressure of the water. The wall is **181 metres** high, measured above the foundation, and about 2.3 kilometres long. It was completed in **2006**. By comparison, the Grande Dixence dam in the Valais is higher at 285 metres but much shorter.

The hydroelectric power station has an installed output of about **22,500 megawatts**. That is more than any other power station in the world. In the machine halls, 32 large turbines and a few smaller ones work. One megawatt is a million watts. The plant therefore supplies as much output as many large power stations put together.

Besides generating electricity, **flood protection** is especially important. On the **middle and lower reaches** of the Yangtze, very many people live in big cities such as Wuhan. In the past, floods there caused great damage again and again. In heavy rain, the reservoir can hold back a lot of water and release it slowly later.

So that cargo ships can continue on the Yangtze, there are two **flights of locks**, one for each direction. Each has **five stages**. A ship is raised or lowered from chamber to chamber until it has overcome the great difference in height. This takes several hours. For smaller ships there is also a faster ship lift.

For the reservoir, about **1.3 million people** had to leave their homes. Towns, villages and ancient cultural sites disappeared under the water. Another problem is the **sediments**: the river brings a lot of sand and mud, which now settles in the reservoir. **Below** the dam this mud is missing, and the **delta** at the mouth near Shanghai is being worn away. Experts are watching the effects closely.

gewusst: At over 6,000 kilometres, the Yangtze is the longest river in Asia.
The idea of a large dam in the three gorges already existed at the beginning of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Gentrification is the name for the change in a city district when it is upgraded and better-off people move in. Rents rise, and some of the former residents can no longer afford their homes.
wichtigste: The term “gentrification” was coined by the sociologist Ruth Glass in London in 1964.
Often pioneers such as students and artists move first into cheap districts of old buildings.
Neil Smith’s rent gap theory explains the process through differences in ground rent.
The most criticised aspect is the displacement of residents on low incomes.
Well-known examples are Prenzlauer Berg in Berlin and Zürich-West.
When many flats are let to holiday guests, this is called touristification.

abschnitte.text: The word **gentrification** comes from the English “gentry”, a name for the lesser nobility. The sociologist **Ruth Glass** used the term “gentrification” in 1964 to describe changes in working-class districts of London. There, better-off families bought old houses, renovated them and moved in. Today the word is used all over the world for similar developments in many cities.

Experts often describe a **phase model**. First **pioneers** such as students and artists move into a cheap, often somewhat run-down district of old buildings. Cafés, studios and shops appear, and the district becomes popular. Then people with higher incomes arrive, buildings are renovated and **rents rise**. Not every district follows exactly this pattern, but it helps to understand the change.

The geographer **Neil Smith** developed the **rent gap theory**. It says: if the rent or income that a plot of land brings today is much lower than the income that would be possible after an upgrade, an investment pays off. Other researchers stress rather that lifestyles are changing and that more people like to live in the centre of the city. Probably both reasons work together.

After German reunification, Berlin’s **Prenzlauer Berg** changed greatly: many old buildings were renovated, and many new, often well-paid families moved in. In Switzerland, **Zürich-West** is often mentioned. There, large factories used to stand, and today there are offices, flats, tower blocks and places to go out. A newer phenomenon is **touristification**: when many flats are let short-term to holiday guests, they are missing for local people.

Supporters say that gentrification brings renovated houses, more shops and safer streets. The most criticised aspect is the **displacement** of people on small incomes. Cities try to steer the change. German cities, for example, use social preservation ordinances to limit luxury renovations in certain districts. In Zürich the city promotes **housing cooperatives**, which let flats without a profit motive.

gewusst: In 2011 the city of Zürich decided by a popular vote that by 2050 a third of rented flats should be non-profit.
The term gentrification is already over 60 years old but is used more often today than ever.

teile.einleitung: Latitude tells you how far north or south of the Equator a place lies. Together with longitude, it lets you pinpoint any spot on Earth exactly.
wichtigste: The Equator has a latitude of 0°, and the North Pole lies at 90° north.
Lines of latitude run parallel to one another and are therefore also called parallels.
Between two lines of latitude one degree apart there are about 111 kilometres.
One degree is divided into 60 minutes of arc.
The Equator is the longest line of latitude.
Switzerland lies roughly between 45.8° and 47.8° north.

abschnitte.text: Imagine the Earth as a ball. The **Equator** divides it into a northern and a southern half and has a latitude of **0°**. From there you count northwards to the **North Pole** at **90° north** and southwards to the South Pole at 90° south. Latitude is really an angle, measured from the centre of the Earth. The bigger the number, the closer a place lies to a pole.

All places with the same latitude lie on one **line of latitude**. Because these circles never meet but run side by side, they are also called **parallels**. The **Equator** is the longest line of latitude, and towards the poles they become ever smaller. Between two lines of latitude one degree apart there are always about **111 kilometres**. Important lines of latitude are the tropics and the polar circles.

For exact figures, one degree is divided into **60 minutes of arc** and one minute into 60 seconds of arc. You can also write latitude as a decimal number, as navigation devices and map apps often do. For example, **Bern** lies at about 46.95° north and 7.44° east. The first number is the latitude, and the second the longitude.

Switzerland lies roughly between **45.8° and 47.8° north**. The southernmost point is in Ticino near Chiasso, and the northernmost in the canton of Schaffhausen. Zürich lies at a good 47° north. At roughly the same latitude on the other side of the world lies the city of **Seattle** in the USA. Places at the same latitude do not always have the same climate, though, because seas, mountains and winds matter too.

gewusst: Sailors used to determine their latitude with the Pole Star: how high it stands above the horizon corresponds roughly to your own latitude.
Degrees of latitude are not quite the same length, because the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.

teile.einleitung: **Favelas** are simple residential districts in Brazilian cities that are often built on steep hills. Especially well known are the favelas of Rio de Janeiro, where very many people live.
wichtigste: Favelas are simple, often self-built residential districts, for example in Rio de Janeiro.
The name originally comes from a plant.
The place of the first favela is regarded as the hill Morro da Providência.
The favela Rocinha is regarded as the most populous in Rio.
Many residents have no title deeds to their land.
Similar settlements are called **bidonvilles** in French-speaking countries and **barriadas** in Peru.

abschnitte.text: A favela is a residential district that often arose without permission. People built their houses themselves, at first from wood and sheet metal, later often from brick. In Rio de Janeiro many favelas lie on steep **hills** in the middle of the city. The houses stand cheek by jowl, linked by narrow lanes and steps. In the favelas there are shops, schools and a lively community life.

The name comes from a prickly **plant** called favela, which grows in the north-east of Brazil. At the end of the 19th century, soldiers returned to Rio from a war in that region. They settled on the hill **Morro da Providência** and named it after a hill on which this plant grew. This place is regarded as the first favela. The most populous favela in Rio today is regarded as **Rocinha**.

Many residents have no **title deed**, that is, no official paper saying that the land belongs to them. Good roads, clean water and a **sewer system** are often lacking. In some favelas drug gangs have great power. From 2008 Rio deployed the **Unidades de Polícia Pacificadora** (Pacifying Police Units). Their aim was to drive the gangs out of the favelas and station police there permanently. The success of these units is still argued over today.

In the past, favelas were sometimes simply demolished and the people resettled. Today the emphasis is often on **slum upgrading**: the districts are improved on the spot with roads, water, electricity and sewers. In this way people can stay in their familiar surroundings. Similar settlements exist all over the world, such as the **bidonvilles** in French-speaking countries or the **barriadas** in Peru.

gewusst: From above, many of Rio’s favelas have one of the finest views of the city and the sea.
Worldwide, a large share of the urban population in poorer countries lives in informal settlements.

teile.einleitung: **Fitz Roy** is a steep granite mountain in Patagonia on the border between Argentina and Chile. With its almost vertical walls, it is among the most difficult and most beautiful climbing mountains in the world.
wichtigste: Fitz Roy is a steep granite mountain in Patagonia.
It is named after Robert FitzRoy, the captain of Darwin’s ship Beagle.
It lies on the border between Argentina and Chile.
The native people called it **Chaltén**, which is said to mean “smoking mountain”.
The first ascent was made in 1952 by two French mountaineers.

abschnitte.text: Fitz Roy is over 3,300 metres high. That is less than many Alpine peaks, but it rises almost vertically out of the landscape. Its walls consist of hard **granite**. Around the summit stand further pointed rock towers and large glaciers. Clouds often hang on the summit, so it looks as if the mountain is smoking. The native people therefore called it **Chaltén**.

The mountain was named in 1877 by the Argentine explorer **Francisco Moreno**. He chose the name of **Robert FitzRoy**, the captain of the ship **Beagle**. On this ship the young **Charles Darwin** had travelled round the world and also visited Patagonia. FitzRoy had carefully surveyed the coasts of South America.

Fitz Roy is regarded as a very difficult mountain. Dangerous above all are the strong **storms** and the quickly changing weather in Patagonia. The **first ascent** was made in 1952 by the Frenchmen **Lionel Terray** and **Guido Magnone**. At the foot of the mountain lies the village of **El Chaltén** in Argentina. It is a popular starting point for walks with a view of the mountain.

gewusst: The outline of Fitz Roy serves as the logo of a well-known outdoor brand.

teile.einleitung: An **estancia** is a large farm in South America, above all in Argentina and Uruguay. On the wide pastures of the Pampas, large herds of cattle, sheep and horses are kept there.
wichtigste: An estancia is a large farm with livestock rearing.
Many estancias lie in the **Pampas**, a wide grassland.
On estancias mainly cattle are kept, but also sheep and horses.
The herders are called **gauchos**.
Some estancias today also welcome holiday guests.

abschnitte.text: The **Pampas** is a huge, flat grassland in Argentina and Uruguay. There are hardly any trees there, but a lot of grass. This makes it ideal for **livestock rearing**. An estancia can be thousands of hectares in size, much bigger than a farm in Switzerland. Argentina is world famous for its beef, which comes to a large extent from such farms. In the cooler south, in Patagonia, many estancias keep mainly **sheep**.

The herders on the estancias are called **gauchos**. They ride horses across the pastures and round up the herds. Their costume with a broad hat, poncho and baggy trousers is well known. In Argentina and Uruguay the gauchos are seen as a symbol of freedom and of life in the countryside. Typical too is **mate**, an herbal tea that is drunk from a cup through a small tube.

Besides the main house, an estancia has stables, paddocks and often accommodation for the workers. Today many farms work with machines, but horses are still important. Some estancias offer **holidays**: guests can ride, watch the work and eat the traditional **asado**, in which meat is grilled over a fire.

gewusst: The word “estancia” comes from Spanish and originally means something like “place of stay”.

teile.einleitung: The Ekati Mine lies in the far north of Canada, in the Northwest Territories. It opened in 1998 and was the country’s first diamond mine.
wichtigste: Ekati lies in the Northwest Territories in the north of Canada.
The mine opened in 1998.
It was Canada’s first diamond mine.
The diamonds are found in **kimberlite**, a rock from volcanic pipes.
Ekati made Canada an important diamond producer.

abschnitte.text: Diamonds form deep in the Earth’s mantle under very high pressure and great heat. In volcanic eruptions long ago, they were torn upwards in narrow tubes. These tubes are called **kimberlite pipes**, after the rock kimberlite. At Ekati such pipes lie in the ancient rock of the **Canadian Shield**, one of the oldest parts of the Earth’s crust.

The mine lies in a lonely area with many lakes, far north of the city of Yellowknife. The winters are long and very cold. There is no permanent road, and material often comes by aeroplane or, in winter, over **ice roads** on frozen lakes. The workers live in a camp for several weeks and then fly home again.

At first the pipes were mined in large open pits, known as **open-cast mining**. Later people also went underground. The rock is crushed, and the diamonds are picked out with machines. After Ekati, further diamond mines were opened nearby, for example Diavik.

gewusst: Before Ekati there was not a single diamond mine in Canada, and today the country is among the big diamond producers in the world.
In winter, lorries drive on roads of thick ice over frozen lakes to the mines.

teile.einleitung: The Gulf of Mexico is a large marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean. It is enclosed by the USA, Mexico and Cuba and is known for oil, fishing and powerful tropical storms.
wichtigste: The USA, Mexico and Cuba border the Gulf of Mexico.
It is connected to the open Atlantic through the Straits of Florida.
Because of the warm water, powerful hurricanes often form there.
A lot of oil is produced from the seabed.
In 2010 the Deepwater Horizon oil rig exploded there.
Every summer an oxygen-poor dead zone forms off the mouth of the Mississippi.

abschnitte.text: The **Gulf of Mexico** is an almost round part of the sea in the south of North America. To the north lies the **USA** with states such as Texas, Louisiana and Florida, to the west and south **Mexico**, and to the south-east **Cuba**. Through the **Straits of Florida** between Florida and Cuba it is connected to the open Atlantic. In the south the Yucatán Channel leads into the Caribbean. The **Mississippi** flows into the gulf. Since 2025 the US government has officially called it the “Gulf of America”, but internationally the old name is still more widely used.

The Mexican port city of **Veracruz** lies on the gulf. Here the Spaniard **Hernán Cortés** landed in 1519 before he conquered the Aztec empire. In Texas lies the city of **Galveston**. In 1900 it was devastated by a huge **hurricane**. The disaster is considered the deadliest natural disaster in the history of the USA.

In summer the **sea water** in the gulf becomes **very warm**. Warm water supplies a lot of energy for tropical storms, which are called **hurricanes** here. That is why powerful storms often move across the gulf. A well-known example is Hurricane Katrina, which hit the city of New Orleans badly in 2005. The hurricane season lasts roughly from June to November.

Under the seabed lie large reserves of **oil** and natural gas. Many **oil rigs** extract them from great depths. In 2010 the **Deepwater Horizon** oil rig **exploded**. For months oil flowed into the sea. It was one of the worst oil disasters in history and harmed fish, birds and beaches.

The Mississippi carries a lot of **fertiliser** from the fields into the sea. As a result, very many algae grow in summer. When they die, bacteria use up the oxygen in the water as they break them down. So every year an **oxygen-poor dead zone** forms off the mouth of the Mississippi, in which fish and other animals can hardly live.

gewusst: The Gulf of Mexico is one of the largest gulfs in the world.
Warm water flows out of the Gulf of Mexico into the Atlantic and forms the start of the Gulf Stream.

teile.einleitung: Geopolitics studies how a country’s position, size and raw materials influence its power and its policies. It is about questions such as: who controls important straits, trade routes and sources of energy? Alliances between states and conflicts over territory are part of it too.
wichtigste: Geopolitics combines geography and politics.
The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the open ocean and is central to oil exports.
The Strait of Malacca between Malaysia and Sumatra is among the busiest sea lanes in the world.
In 1904 Halford Mackinder put forward the Heartland theory about the importance of Eurasia.
The “S” in BRICS stands for South Africa.
ASEAN is a community of states in South-East Asia.
Switzerland has been a full member of the UN since 2002.

abschnitte.text: **Geopolitics** asks how geography influences the power of states. Important are the position on seas or mountains, the size of a country, its population and its **raw materials** such as oil, gas or rare metals. Countries with access to the sea can, for example, trade more easily. That is why states sometimes quarrel over islands, borders or waterways.

A **strait** is a narrow waterway between two landmasses. The **Strait of Hormuz** links the Persian Gulf with the open ocean, and a large part of the oil traded worldwide is carried through it. The **Strait of Malacca** between Malaysia and the island of Sumatra is one of the busiest sea lanes in the world. Artificial canals such as the Suez Canal and the Panama Canal are also very important for world trade.

The British geographer **Halford Mackinder** presented the **Heartland theory** in 1904. He argued that whoever controlled the core area of Eurasia could rule the world. This idea influenced the thinking of many politicians in the 20th century. Today such theories are viewed more critically, because trade, technology and alliances also mean a great deal of power.

States join together to have more influence. The group **BRICS** is named after Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, and since 2024 further countries have joined. **ASEAN** is a community of states in South-East Asia, for example Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia. Further examples are the European Union and the military alliance NATO.

Some regions of the world are especially affected by crises. The **Sahel** is the transition from the Sahara to the savannah, where many people suffer from drought, poverty and armed conflicts. Interest in the Arctic is also growing, because the melting ice makes new shipping routes and raw materials reachable. Water from large rivers such as the Nile also leads to disputes between countries.

Switzerland is a small country with no access to the sea and has long been **neutral**. After a popular vote in March 2002, it became a full member of the **UN** in the same year. In Geneva there is a major seat of the United Nations, and many international organisations have their headquarters there. Switzerland often offers its **good offices**, for example as a place for peace talks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow waterway between two pieces of land.
A substance from nature, for example oil, gas or copper.
A country does not take part in the wars of other countries.
A union of states that support each other.

gewusst: At its narrowest point the Strait of Hormuz is only about 40 kilometres wide.
In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a member of the UN Security Council for the first time.

teile.einleitung: By aeroplane you can quickly reach distant countries. A flight begins at the airport and follows fixed procedures so that everyone arrives safely.
wichtigste: To board you need a boarding pass.
The pilots sit at the front in the cockpit.
Cabin crew look after the passengers.
At take-off and landing you must have your seat belt fastened.
On long routes big aeroplanes fly about 10 kilometres high.
The largest passenger aeroplane in the world is the Airbus A380.

abschnitte.text: The largest airport in Switzerland is in **Zurich**, and other important ones are Geneva and Basel. First you hand in your big suitcase. It travels in the belly of the aeroplane. A small bag you may take to your seat as **hand luggage**. At the **security check**, bags and people are scanned.

On the **boarding pass** are your name, the flight number and your seat. It is checked when you board at the gate. For journeys abroad you also need a valid **passport** or an identity card. Which document is needed depends on the destination.

At the very front of the aeroplane is the **cockpit**. There the pilot and co-pilot sit with all the instruments. In the cabin, **cabin crew** work. They show the safety rules before take-off, bring food and drinks and help with questions. In an emergency they know exactly what to do.

At take-off and landing, every passenger has to fasten the **seat belt**. On long routes big aeroplanes usually fly **10 to 12 kilometres** high. There the air is thin, and the aeroplanes make good progress. Outside it is icy cold, but inside the cabin it is pleasant. When climbing and descending you often feel the pressure in your ears.

Anyone flying from Zurich to **New York** crosses the **Atlantic**. The flight takes about eight to nine hours. The largest passenger aeroplane in the world is the **Airbus A380**. It has two decks over the whole length and can carry over 500 people.

gewusst: Because you fly west with the time, you land in New York by local time only a few hours later than when you took off in Zurich.
Liquids in hand luggage are allowed at the security check only in small containers.

teile.einleitung: On 19 September 1985 a strong earthquake struck Mexico City. Although the epicentre lay about 350 km away on the Pacific coast, many buildings collapsed in the capital. The reason lies in the soft ground beneath the city.
wichtigste: The quake occurred on **19 September 1985**.
The epicentre lay about **350 km** away on the Pacific coast.
Mexico City stands on the deposits of a **former lake**.
The soft, wet soils **amplified** the earthquake waves.
Above all **medium-rise buildings** collapsed.

abschnitte.titel: A city on an old lake
abschnitte.text: Mexico City lies in a high valley in which there used to be large lakes. The Aztecs already built their capital **Tenochtitlan** on an island in **Lake Texcoco**. Later the lakes were almost completely drained. Beneath large parts of today’s city there are therefore thick layers of soft, water-saturated **clay**.

When the earthquake waves reached the city from the coast, they had already become weaker. But the soft **lake sediments** set them swinging again, like a pudding that you shake. The ground swung back and forth for a long time and strongly. Buildings of a certain height, above all **medium-rise buildings**, swung in the same rhythm and collapsed. Experts call this **resonance**.

Several thousand people died in the quake, and many buildings were destroyed. Afterwards the **building regulations** in Mexico were tightened so that houses withstand earthquakes better. Later an **early warning system** was also set up: measuring stations on the coast report a quake, and sirens howl in the capital before the waves arrive. Every year on 19 September, people practise in a large **earthquake drill** what to do in a real emergency.

gewusst: On 19 September 2017, of all days, the anniversary and shortly after the drill, another strong earthquake struck Mexico City.
Because Mexico City stands on soft lake ground, some districts still sink a little further every year.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is constantly turning on itself, like a spinning top. This turning is called the **Earth’s rotation** and ensures that we have day and night.
wichtigste: The Earth turns once on itself in about 24 hours.
It turns around an imaginary line, the **Earth’s axis**.
The direction of turning is from west to east.
On the side facing the Sun it is day, and on the side facing away it is night.
We do not feel the turning because we turn with it.
Measured against the distant stars, one turn takes about 23 hours and 56 minutes.

abschnitte.titel: The Earth as a spinning top
abschnitte.text: The Earth turns around the **Earth’s axis**, an imaginary line from the North Pole through the centre of the Earth to the South Pole. For one whole turn it needs about **24 hours**, that is, a day with its night. In a week it therefore turns seven times on itself. The turning goes from **west to east**. Seen from the North Pole, the Earth turns anticlockwise.

The Sun can only ever light one half of the Earth. Where it shines, it is light and **day**, and on the other side it is **night**. When it is midday in Switzerland, it is the middle of the night on the opposite side of the Earth. Because the Earth turns east, we see the Sun rise in the east and set in the west. With a torch and a globe you can act this out nicely at home.

At the equator, the ground moves because of the turning at about 1,670 kilometres per hour. In Switzerland it is still about 1,100 kilometres per hour. Even so we feel nothing of it, because everything turns with it: the ground, the houses, the air and we ourselves. It is similar in a smoothly moving train, in which you can put a glass of water on the table.

If the turning is measured against the distant stars, it takes only about **23 hours and 56 minutes**. This is called a **sidereal day**. Because the Earth is travelling round the Sun at the same time, it has to turn a little further until the Sun stands in the same place again. This gives the **solar day** of 24 hours. If the Earth did not turn at all, day and night would each be very long, because there would be only one change per year.

gewusst: In 1851 Léon Foucault proved in Paris with a long pendulum that the Earth turns.
The turning of the Earth is getting very slowly slower, mainly because of the tidal forces of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: The Earth’s crust consists of large plates that move slowly. At a divergent plate boundary, two plates drift apart. Hot rock rises into the gap, and new crust is formed.
wichtigste: At divergent plate boundaries, two plates move away from each other.
In the ocean, new oceanic crust forms as a result.
Another name is constructive plate boundary.
The magma forms mainly through decompression melting.
The further you move from the ridge, the older the crust is.
Harry Hess published the model of seafloor spreading in 1962.

abschnitte.text: At a **divergent plate boundary**, two plates of the Earth move apart, usually only a few centimetres a year. Because new crust is built in the process, it is also called a **constructive plate boundary**. In the ocean, long mountain chains form under the water, the **mid-ocean ridges**. The best known is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Among the fastest is the **East Pacific Rise**, where the plates separate much more quickly.

Beneath the ridges, hot rock from the Earth’s mantle slowly rises. The higher it gets, the less pressure there is on it. As a result, part of it begins to melt, although it hardly gets any hotter. This process is called **decompression melting**. The magma pushes into cracks and hardens into new oceanic crust made of **basalt**. When lava emerges on the seabed, it cools quickly in the cold water and forms rounded shapes, called **pillow lava**.

In **1962** the American geologist **Harry Hess** published the model of **seafloor spreading**. Important proof soon followed: on the seabed, **magnetic stripes** were found, arranged as mirror images on both sides of the ridges. They arise because the Earth’s magnetic field reverses again and again, and the cooling rock stores the direction at the time. It also turned out that the age of the crust **increases** the further you move from the ridge.

At the spreading ridges, seawater seeps into the ground, is strongly heated and shoots out again. In this way hot springs form on the seabed. Some give off dark, mineral-rich water and are therefore called **black smokers**. Around them live astonishing animals such as tube worms, mussels and crabs, although no sunlight reaches there.
