Divergent plate boundaries also exist on the continents. In **East Africa**, the continent is slowly tearing open along the East African Rift. On **Iceland**, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge even rises out of the sea. There, in Thingvellir National Park, you can walk in a rift between the North American and the Eurasian plates. Iceland therefore has many volcanoes and hot springs.

gewusst: The oldest parts of today’s ocean floors are only about 180 million years old, much younger than some rocks on the continents.
Together, the mid-ocean ridges form the longest mountain range on Earth, almost entirely under water.
Because of the spreading, the Atlantic grows a few centimetres wider every year.

teile.einleitung: The destination life cycle is a model from tourism research. It describes how a holiday resort develops over time: from discovery through the boom to decline or renewal. The geographer Richard Butler made it well known.
wichtigste: Richard Butler published the model in 1980.
It builds on the product life cycle from economics.
The phases are called exploration, involvement, development, consolidation and stagnation.
In the development phase, outside investors and hotel chains increasingly take control.
In stagnation, capacity limits have been reached and the image seems out of date.
After that comes either decline or rejuvenation.
Atlantic City is an example of rejuvenation through gambling casinos.

abschnitte.text: In 1980 the geographer **Richard Butler** published the **Tourism Area Life Cycle** model, in German **Destinationslebenszyklus**. A **destination** is a place to travel to, for example a seaside resort or a mountain village. Butler built on the **product life cycle** from economics. This describes how a product is introduced, grows, reaches its peak and loses importance again.

In the first phase, **exploration**, only a few travellers come. There are hardly any facilities for guests, and the visitors live closely with the locals. In the **involvement** phase, local people begin to offer the first **accommodation** and **services**. Small guesthouses, restaurants and the first advertising appear.

In the **development phase**, guest numbers rise sharply. **Outside investors** and **hotel chains** increasingly take control. Large hotels and new roads are built. After that comes **consolidation**: the number of guests grows only slowly, but tourism has become the most important branch of the economy in the place.

In **stagnation**, the **capacity limits** have been reached. There are too many guests, too much traffic or too little space. The hotels have grown older, and the **image** seems **out of date**. New guests stay away, and many come only out of habit.

After stagnation there are, according to Butler, two possibilities: **decline** or **rejuvenation**. In decline, guests stay away and hotels close. In rejuvenation, the place reinvents itself with new attractions. As an example Butler named **Atlantic City** in the USA, which attracted many guests again by allowing **gambling casinos**. Holiday resorts in the Swiss Alps also keep trying to renew themselves with new offers in summer and winter.

gewusst: Butler’s model is among the most frequently cited models in tourism research.
Not every place goes through all the phases, and some places deliberately stay small and quiet.

teile.einleitung: In **remote sensing**, the Earth is studied from a distance, usually with satellites or aeroplanes. In this way forests, fields, glaciers and cities can be observed without being on the spot.
wichtigste: In 1972 Landsat 1 was launched as the first of a long US series of civilian Earth observation satellites.
The Sentinel satellites belong to the EU programme **Copernicus**.
Active systems send out radiation themselves and measure the echo, while passive ones measure existing light.
Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) supplies images even through clouds and at night.
**Lidar** produces very accurate height models with laser pulses.
The vegetation index NDVI compares red and near infrared.

abschnitte.text: In 1972 **Landsat 1** was launched, the first of a long series of civilian Earth observation satellites of the USA. Since then the Landsat images have shown how the Earth is changing. Today the EU runs the **Copernicus** programme with the **Sentinel satellites**. Their data is freely accessible to everyone. Researchers use it to observe, for example, forest fires, floods or melting glaciers.

**Passive** systems measure the sunlight that is reflected by the Earth, similar to a camera. **Active** systems send out radiation themselves and measure the **echo**. One example is **synthetic aperture radar**, SAR for short. Because it sends out its own microwaves, it supplies images even through **clouds** and at **night**. Another active method is **lidar**: laser pulses are sent from an aeroplane to the ground, producing very accurate height models.

A satellite image consists of many small picture points, the **pixels**. The **spatial resolution** says what area of ground a pixel covers. At a resolution of ten metres, a pixel shows a square of ten by ten metres. On it you can recognise fields and roads, but not individual people. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Topography **swisstopo** uses aerial photographs and lidar for accurate maps and height models.

Satellites also see light that is invisible to our eyes, such as the **near infrared**. Healthy plants reflect a lot of near infrared but little red light. The vegetation index **NDVI** compares exactly these two ranges and so shows how healthy the plants are. In a classic **infrared false-colour image**, healthy vegetation therefore appears bright red. In this way experts can see, for example, where fields are suffering from dryness.

gewusst: Some satellites photograph every place on Earth afresh every few days.
With lidar you can measure the ground through forests and so discover old paths or walls.

teile.einleitung: Liquefied natural gas, LNG for short, is natural gas that has been cooled so strongly that it becomes liquid. In this way it can be carried across the seas by large tanker ships.
wichtigste: LNG stands for “Liquefied Natural Gas”.
Natural gas becomes liquid at about minus 162 degrees Celsius.
As a liquid it needs about 600 times less space.
In 2023 the USA was the largest exporter of LNG.
In the importing country, LNG is turned back into gas at terminals.
Switzerland gets its natural gas mainly through pipelines from neighbouring countries.

abschnitte.text: Natural gas consists mainly of **methane**. Methane boils at about **minus 162 degrees Celsius**. If natural gas is cooled that much, it becomes liquid. It then needs only about **one six-hundredth** of the space. This is what makes transport by ship economical in the first place. In well-insulated tanks the LNG stays liquid.

Special **LNG tankers** bring the liquefied gas from the producing countries to the customers. Although the tanks are insulated, some heat always gets in. A small part of the cargo therefore evaporates. Many tankers use this **boil-off gas** as fuel for their propulsion.

Thanks to **shale gas** and new terminals on the Gulf Coast, the **USA** became the largest exporter in 2023, ahead of Qatar and Australia. A large part went to Europe. **Qatar** liquefies its natural gas from the huge North Field at **Ras Laffan**. This is one of the largest LNG centres in the world.

In the importing country the LNG goes into a **terminal**. There it is warmed and turned back into gas. This is called **regasification**. Afterwards it flows into the pipeline network as ordinary natural gas. An **FSRU** is a floating terminal that stores and regasifies gas. From the end of 2022 Germany used such a facility in **Wilhelmshaven**, because it is ready faster than a terminal on land.

**Japan** is an island nation with no gas pipelines to other countries. It has to bring in almost all its natural gas by ship and has been one of the largest LNG importers for decades. **Switzerland** has no access to the sea and no LNG terminal of its own. Its gas comes through **high-pressure pipelines** such as the Transitgas pipeline. Part of it can nevertheless come from LNG that was landed in neighbouring countries.

gewusst: Liquid natural gas is colourless and looks like water.
The first LNG tanker was a converted cargo ship, whereas today there are purpose-built ships with huge spherical or box-shaped tanks.

teile.einleitung: **Food security** means that all people have enough safe and healthy food at all times. The world is still far from this, because hunger remains a big problem to this day.
wichtigste: The definition in common use today was set in 1996 at the World Food Summit in Rome.
The FAO distinguishes four dimensions: availability, access, utilisation and stability.
The UN Sustainable Development Goal 2 aims to end hunger by 2030.
According to the UN report SOFI 2025, about 670 million people suffered from hunger in 2024.
The UN World Food Programme received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
In 2024 Switzerland produced about half of its food itself.

abschnitte.text: At the **World Food Summit** in Rome in 1996, states agreed on a definition: food security exists when all people have access at all times to enough safe and nutritious food to lead an active and healthy life. The **FAO**, the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, distinguishes four dimensions here. These are **availability**, **access**, **utilisation** and **stability**.

**Availability** means that enough food is produced or imported in the first place. **Access** means that people can also buy it or grow it themselves. **Utilisation** is about the food being healthy, prepared cleanly and absorbed well by the body. **Stability** means that supply stays secure even in crises, droughts or when prices are high.

According to the UN food report **SOFI 2025**, about 670 million people suffered from hunger in 2024. Besides visible hunger there is **hidden hunger**: people eat enough calories, but they lack vitamins and minerals. The UN’s **Sustainable Development Goal 2** aims to end hunger by 2030. The UN **World Food Programme** received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020 for its work against hunger.

Switzerland cannot produce all its food itself. In 2024 its **self-sufficiency rate** was about 50 per cent, and the other half is imported. For crises the federal government holds **compulsory stocks**, for example of grain, sugar, rice and cooking oil. A different view is held by the concept of **food sovereignty** of the small farmers’ movement La Via Campesina: peoples should be able to decide their own agricultural and food policy.

gewusst: Worldwide, a large part of the food is never eaten, because it spoils on the way or is thrown away.
Since 2017 food security has been a goal in the Swiss Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Gabriel García Márquez was a writer from Colombia. He is one of the best-known authors of Latin America and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.
wichtigste: García Márquez was born in 1927 in Aracataca in Colombia.
His most famous novel is “One Hundred Years of Solitude”.
He is regarded as an important representative of magical realism.
In 1982 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
He died in 2014 in Mexico City.

abschnitte.text: **Gabriel García Márquez** was born in 1927 in **Aracataca**, a small town in the north of Colombia. As a child he lived with his grandparents, who told him many stories. Later he worked for a long time as a **journalist**. Friends and readers affectionately called him **“Gabo”**.

In 1967 his most famous novel, **“One Hundred Years of Solitude”**, appeared. It tells the story of a family over several generations in the imaginary village of **Macondo**. In the book, marvellous things happen that are told as a matter of course. This way of telling a story is called **magical realism**. The novel was translated into a great many languages.

In 1982 García Márquez received the **Nobel Prize in Literature**. Other well-known books are **“Chronicle of a Death Foretold”** and **“Love in the Time of Cholera”**. He spent many years in **Mexico** and died in 2014 in Mexico City. Other Latin American Nobel laureates include the Chilean Pablo Neruda and the Peruvian Mario Vargas Llosa.

gewusst: The village of Macondo does not really exist, but it recalls Aracataca, the author’s birthplace.

teile.einleitung: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan and one of the best-known mountains in the world. It is a volcano with an almost perfect cone shape.
wichtigste: Mount Fuji is 3,776 metres high and the highest mountain in Japan.
It stands on Honshu, the largest island of Japan.
It lies about 100 kilometres from Tokyo.
The last eruption was in 1707.
On its northern foot lie the Fuji Five Lakes.
For many people in Japan it is a sacred mountain.

abschnitte.text: **Mount Fuji** stands in **Japan** on the island of **Honshu**, the largest island of the country. It is **3,776 metres** high. That makes it lower than the Matterhorn at 4,478 metres. Mount Fuji looks like a large, almost perfectly even **cone**. In winter it often wears a white **snow cap**. This is how it is seen in many pictures.

Mount Fuji is a **volcano**. It has grown layer by layer through many eruptions. The last eruption was in **1707**. At that time ash fell as far as the area of present-day Tokyo. Since then the volcano has been quiet, but it is still regarded as active and is monitored.

Mount Fuji is a **landmark** of Japan. For many people it is a **sacred mountain**. In Japanese it is often called **Fuji-san**. The character 山 is read “san” here and means **mountain**. It is therefore not the polite form of address for people. The artist Hokusai made the mountain world famous with his woodblock prints. Since 2013 Mount Fuji has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

On the northern foot of Mount Fuji lie the **Fuji Five Lakes**. From there you have a lovely view of the mountain. Mount Fuji lies about **100 kilometres** from **Tokyo**. On clear days you can even see it from the city. In summer very many people climb to the summit every year.

gewusst: Many people climb Mount Fuji at night to see the sunrise from the summit.
Outside the summer months the climb is dangerous because of snow and cold.

teile.einleitung: An edge city is a large centre with offices, shopping centres and companies on the edge of a big city. It often arises where there used to be fields, usually at motorway junctions. The American journalist Joel Garreau made the term well known.
wichtigste: Joel Garreau made the term “edge city” known in 1991 with a book.
An edge city has more jobs than bedrooms.
Garreau required at least 5 million square feet of office space.
Edge cities often arise at motorway junctions in the surroundings of big cities.
Tysons Corner near Washington D.C. is regarded as a prime example.
The development is part of post-suburbanisation.
In Switzerland, the Glattal near Zurich is often named as an example.

abschnitte.text: The English term **edge city** means roughly “city on the edge”. It refers to a large centre with offices, shops and companies outside the old city centre. The term was made known by the American journalist **Joel Garreau** in **1991** with his book about these new places. He observed that in the USA more and more jobs were no longer in the city centre but in the **surrounding area**.

Garreau named clear features for an edge city. It needs at least **5 million square feet of office space**, which is about 460,000 square metres. Large areas for shops are added to this. There are **more jobs than bedrooms** there, so many people commute in every morning. People see the place as a centre in its own right. In addition, a few decades earlier the area was not yet a city.

Edge cities typically arise at **motorway junctions** in the surroundings of big cities. Land is cheaper there, and the place is easy to reach by car. **Tysons Corner** in the state of Virginia, near Washington D.C., is regarded as a **prime example**. There used to be a road junction with fields, and today there are tall buildings and large shopping centres. First people moved from the cities to the suburbs, then jobs and shops followed. This phase is called **post-suburbanisation**.

In the German-speaking world, the architect **Thomas Sieverts** used the term **Zwischenstadt** (“in-between city”) in 1997 to describe a similar landscape that is neither properly city nor country. In Switzerland the **Glattal** in the north of Zurich is often named as an example. Around the airport, Wallisellen and Opfikon, many offices, hotels and shopping centres were built. Unlike many American edge cities, public transport was also greatly expanded there, for example with the Glattal light railway.

gewusst: Garreau counted about 200 such edge cities in the USA as early as the beginning of the 1990s.
Many edge cities have no municipal administration of their own, because they are spread over several municipalities.

teile.einleitung: The **epicentre** is the point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. There the shaking is usually strongest. With measuring stations and a little calculation, it is possible to find out where it lies.
wichtigste: The focus in the depths is called the **hypocentre**.
The epicentre lies on the surface exactly above it.
Near the epicentre the waves are weakened the least.
**P waves** arrive first, then the **S waves**.
S waves do not pass through liquids.
To locate it, at least **three** measuring stations are needed.
Quakes with a focus down to about 70 km depth count as **shallow**.

abschnitte.text: An earthquake begins deep in the Earth, where rock suddenly breaks or shifts. This place is called the **hypocentre** or earthquake focus. From there the waves spread out in all directions. The **epicentre** lies directly above it on the Earth’s surface. Because earthquake waves lose strength with distance, the damage is usually greatest near it. If the focus is at most about 70 km deep, this is called a **shallow quake**, which often destroys especially much.

**P waves** or primary waves are the fastest earthquake waves. They push and pull the rock in the direction of travel, so they are always recorded first. **S waves** are slower **shear waves** that move the rock back and forth sideways. Liquids cannot be sheared, so S waves do not pass through the liquid outer core of the Earth.

abschnitte.titel: Working out the distance from the time
abschnitte.text: Because the two kinds of wave travel at different speeds, they arrive with a time gap. The further away the epicentre, the bigger this gap becomes. An example: P waves travel at 6 km/s, S waves at 3.5 km/s, and the station measures a 20-second difference. Then d divided by 3.5 minus d divided by 6 equals 20. This gives a distance of about **168 km**.

A single station knows only the distance, that is, a circle around itself. A second station gives a second circle, which cuts the first at two points. Only with **three stations** do all the circles meet at a single point: the epicentre. In Switzerland this is done by the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich with many measuring stations.

The **epicentral distance** is the distance from a measuring station to the epicentre on the Earth’s surface. For quakes far away it is often given in **degrees**, as an angle from the centre of the Earth. One degree of the Earth’s circumference corresponds to about 111 km. A distance of 30 degrees is therefore about 30 times 111 km, roughly **3,300 km**.

gewusst: Because S waves do not pass through the outer core, researchers know that it is liquid, although nobody has ever been there.
The word “epicentre” comes from Greek: “epi” means “on” or “above”.

teile.einleitung: Gabon is a country on the west coast of Central Africa. It is largely covered by tropical rainforest and is crossed by the Equator.
wichtigste: The capital of Gabon is Libreville.
More than 70 per cent of the area is rainforest.
The most important river is the Ogooué.
The official language is French, and Gabon became independent in 1960.
Oil brings in most of the export earnings.
In Lambaréné, Albert Schweitzer founded a jungle hospital.

abschnitte.text: Gabon lies on the **Atlantic** and is crossed by the **Equator**. It is among the most heavily forested countries on Earth. More than **70 per cent** of the area is **tropical rainforest**. The most important river is the **Ogooué**. It is about 1,200 kilometres long and drains the largest part of the country. Among its largest tributaries is the Ivindo.

The capital **Libreville** lies on the coast in the north-west. The name means “free town”, because freed slaves were settled here. Gabon was a **French colony** and became **independent in 1960**. That is why **French** is the official language. In everyday life many people also speak Bantu languages such as **Fang**.

Gabon is rich in raw materials. About four fifths of the export earnings come from **oil**. In addition, **manganese** and **timber** are exported. At **Oklo**, something special was discovered in 1972: around two billion years ago, chain reactions ran by themselves in uranium deposits there. They were **natural nuclear reactors** from primeval times.

Gabon has many **national parks**. In **Loango National Park** the rainforest borders directly on the sea. That is why you can see **elephants**, buffalo and hippopotamuses on the sandy beach there. In the rainforest there are also gorillas and chimpanzees.

The doctor **Albert Schweitzer** opened a **jungle hospital** in **Lambaréné** on the Ogooué in 1913. There he treated many sick people from the whole area. Schweitzer was also a theologian and organist. For his work he later received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The hospital still exists today.

gewusst: The natural nuclear reactors of Oklo are the only known ones on Earth.
Albert Schweitzer came from Alsace and was a famous organ player.

teile.einleitung: A globe is a scaled-down model of the Earth in the shape of a ball. It shows continents, seas and countries in their correct shape and position in relation to each other. Because the Earth itself is round, a globe is more accurate than any flat map.
wichtigste: A globe is a model of the Earth.
It has the shape of a ball.
The line around the middle of the globe is called the equator.
A globe turns on a tilted axis, just like the Earth.
Lines of latitude and longitude help to find every place.
The oldest surviving globe of the Earth is the “Erdapfel” by Martin Behaim of Nuremberg.
On a flat map, areas are always slightly distorted, but not on a globe.

abschnitte.text: A **globe** is a ball-shaped model of the Earth, greatly reduced in size. The word comes from Latin and means ball. A globe shows continents, oceans, countries, mountains and cities. There are also celestial globes with constellations and globes of other heavenly bodies such as the Moon or Mars.

Around the middle of the globe runs the **equator**, which divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres. Parallel to it run the **lines of latitude**. From pole to pole run the **lines of longitude**, or meridians, and the prime meridian passes through Greenwich near London. With these lines you can give exact coordinates to any place on Earth.

A globe is usually mounted on a stand and can be turned around an **axis**. This axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, just like the real axis of the Earth. This tilt is the reason why there are seasons on Earth. If you turn the globe all the way round once, you show one rotation of the Earth, which in reality takes one day.

The Earth is round, but a map is flat. If you want to show a ball on paper, you have to distort it, just as you cannot press an orange peel flat without it tearing. On many world maps, Greenland or Antarctica therefore look far too big. On a globe the shapes, areas and distances are right, but it is awkward to handle and shows only a few details.

The ancient Greeks already knew that the Earth is a sphere. The oldest surviving globe of the Earth is the **Erdapfel** (“Earth Apple”), which Martin Behaim had made in Nuremberg in 1492. America is not on it yet, because Columbus only arrived there in the same year. Today there are illuminated globes, talking globes and digital globes on the computer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, the same distance from both poles.
A line parallel to the equator.
A line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole.
The imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.

gewusst: The equator is about 40,000 kilometres long.
A globe at a scale of 1:40 million has a circumference of about one metre.

teile.einleitung: The three-sector hypothesis divides the economy into three large areas: agriculture, industry and services. It describes how people’s work shifts from one area to the next in the course of development. The French economist Jean Fourastié made it well known.
wichtigste: The primary sector includes agriculture, forestry and fishing.
The secondary sector includes industry, crafts and construction.
The tertiary sector includes services.
Jean Fourastié of France made the hypothesis known in 1949.
Economies develop from an agrarian society through an industrial society to a service society.
The shift towards services is called tertiarisation.
In Switzerland today, under 5 per cent work in the primary sector.

abschnitte.text: The **primary sector** obtains raw materials from nature: **agriculture, forestry and fishing**, and often mining too. The **secondary sector** turns raw materials into products. This includes industry, crafts and energy supply. In Swiss statistics, **construction** also counts here. The **tertiary sector** covers all **services**, such as trade, banks, hospitals, schools and tourism.

The French economist **Jean Fourastié** published a book in 1949 that became known in German under the title **“Die grosse Hoffnung des 20. Jahrhunderts”** (The Great Hope of the 20th Century). In it he described how employment shifts between the sectors. Similar ideas had already been put forward before him by the economists **Allan Fisher** and **Colin Clark**. But Fourastié made the model especially well known.

According to the hypothesis, economies go through three stages. First, most people work in agriculture, which is the **agrarian society**. With machines and factories, the **industrial society** arises. Later, most people work in the services area, which is called the **service society**. This shift is called **tertiarisation**. When the share of industry falls, this is called **deindustrialisation**.

Fourastié explained the shift through **technical progress**. In agriculture and industry, machines can take over a great deal of work, so fewer and fewer people are needed there. In services, progress is, according to Fourastié, **the smallest**: a teacher, a hairdresser or a nurse cannot simply work faster. For this reason the tertiary sector takes up the most workers in the long run.

Switzerland is a typical **service society**. In the 2020s, **under 5 per cent** of employed people work in the primary sector. About a fifth work in the secondary sector, for example in the watch, machinery or pharmaceutical industries. The great majority, about three quarters, work in the tertiary sector. About 200 years ago it was still the other way round: then most people lived from farming.

gewusst: Some experts add a fourth, quaternary sector to the model for information and knowledge work.
Although only a few people in Switzerland work in agriculture, thanks to machines they produce much more than in the past.

teile.einleitung: The Earth can be divided into two halves, the hemispheres. The **equator** separates the northern hemisphere from the southern hemisphere. Switzerland lies in the northern hemisphere.
wichtigste: The **equator** divides the Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.
Switzerland lies in the **northern hemisphere**.
The **South Pole** lies in the southern hemisphere.
Most people live in the northern hemisphere.
The whole of **Europe** lies in the northern hemisphere.
**Argentina** and Australia lie in the southern hemisphere.
In the northern hemisphere, the **Pole Star** points roughly north.

abschnitte.text: The **equator** is an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth. It divides it into two equal halves. North of it lies the **northern hemisphere** with the North Pole, and south of it the **southern hemisphere** with the **South Pole**. The Earth can also be divided into an eastern and a western hemisphere, but for that you need a different line from pole to pole.

Switzerland lies far north of the equator, that is, in the **northern hemisphere**. The whole of **Europe** and North America also lie there. In the northern hemisphere there is much more land, so almost **nine out of ten** people live there. In the southern hemisphere lie, for example, **Argentina** in the south of South America, Australia and **Antarctica**.

abschnitte.titel: Animals in the north and in the south
abschnitte.text: The **polar bear** lives wild in the **Arctic** around the North Pole. At the South Pole there are no polar bears. Penguins live there instead. The **kangaroo** lives wild only in Australia and New Guinea, in the southern hemisphere. It hops on its strong hind legs.

For us the Sun stands in the **south** at midday. In **Sydney** in Australia it is the other way round: there the midday Sun stands in the **north**. The seasons are also reversed. When it is winter for us, it is summer in the southern hemisphere. That is why many people in Australia celebrate Christmas in warm weather, sometimes on the beach.

In the northern hemisphere, the **Pole Star** helps with finding your way. It stands almost exactly above the North Pole. Anyone who looks at it is looking north. In the southern hemisphere the Pole Star cannot be seen. There people find their way by a different constellation, the **Southern Cross**.

gewusst: The Southern Cross is so important that it appears on the flag of Australia.
At the equator, day and night are almost the same length all year round.

teile.einleitung: The Galápagos cormorant is a seabird that lives only on the Galápagos Islands. It is something quite special: it cannot fly.
wichtigste: The Galápagos cormorant lives only on the Galápagos Islands.
Its wings are so short that it cannot fly.
It is the only flightless cormorant in the world.
It dives to hunt fish and other sea creatures.
There are only a few of these birds, so it is protected.

abschnitte.titel: A bird that does not fly
abschnitte.text: Most cormorants are good fliers. The **Galápagos cormorant**, by contrast, has very **short wings**. With them it cannot take off. It is the **only flightless cormorant** in the world. After diving it spreads its small wings to dry them in the sun.

The Galápagos cormorant looks for its food in the sea. It **dives** and hunts **fish**, eels and squid on the sea floor. For swimming it uses mainly its strong **feet** with webbed toes. Because it used to have hardly any enemies on land on the islands, it no longer needed to fly. Over many generations the wings became smaller.

The bird lives only on the coasts of the islands of **Fernandina** and **Isabela**. There are only a few of these birds. Dangers are, for example, introduced animals such as dogs and cats, as well as years with little food in the sea. The Galápagos cormorant is therefore **strictly protected**.

gewusst: The Galápagos cormorant is an example of how animals on remote islands adapt to their surroundings.

teile.einleitung: A hub is a large airport through which an airline bundles many of its connections. Travellers arrive there and change to a connecting flight. In this way very many destinations can be linked with only a few routes.
wichtigste: The network model with central airports is called the hub-and-spoke system.
At a hub, many travellers change planes.
Atlanta had the most passengers in the world in 2024.
Dubai counted the most international passengers in 2024.
Arrivals and departures are bundled into waves.
The minimum connecting time is the shortest permitted time for changing planes.
For Switzerland, Zurich is the most important hub.

abschnitte.text: The model is called the **hub-and-spoke system**, as with a wheel. The hub is the central airport, and the spokes are the routes to many other airports. Instead of linking every city directly with every other, all flights go to the hub. There the travellers change planes. In this way an airline needs far fewer routes and can fill its aircraft better.

For changing planes to work, many flights arrive at a hub shortly after one another and take off again soon afterwards. This bundling is called the **wave system**. For every airport a **minimum connecting time** applies. It gives the **shortest permitted time for changing** between two flights. In this time, travellers and luggage must make it to the next aircraft.

In **2024**, **Atlanta** airport in the USA had the most passengers in the world. The airline Delta is based there, and many travellers change to domestic flights. The most **international** passengers in the same year were counted at **Dubai**, the hub of Emirates. Other big hubs include London Heathrow, Paris and Frankfurt.

Cities such as **Dubai**, **Doha** and **Istanbul** lie between Europe, Asia and Africa. From there you can reach many parts of the world with a single flight. They are therefore especially well suited to **transfer traffic**. **Qatar Airways** uses Hamad International Airport in Doha as its hub. In 2019, Turkish Airlines moved from the old Atatürk Airport to the new, much larger **Istanbul Airport**.

In Switzerland, **Zurich** airport is the most important hub. The airline Swiss has its base here. Many travellers from other countries change to long-haul flights in Zurich. Not all airlines work with hubs: many low-cost airlines mainly offer direct connections between two cities. A disadvantage of hubs is that delays quickly affect many connections.

gewusst: With ten cities, all the direct connections would need 45 routes, but through a hub in one of the cities, 9 are enough.
Istanbul Airport was planned so that it could one day be among the largest airports in the world.

teile.einleitung: Florida is a state in the south-east of the USA. It lies on a large peninsula between two seas and is known for sun, beaches and rocket launches.
wichtigste: Florida is a peninsula between the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico.
The capital is Tallahassee, not the better-known Miami.
Many NASA rockets launch from Cape Canaveral.
In the south lies the island chain of the Florida Keys as far as Key West.
Florida is called the “Sunshine State” because of its weather.
In the south lie the swamp landscapes of the Everglades.

abschnitte.text: Florida juts south into the sea as a long **peninsula**. To the east lies the **Atlantic**, and to the west the **Gulf of Mexico**. The land is very flat, and there are no mountains. In the south lie the **Everglades**, a huge area of swamp, grass and water. Alligators and many water birds, for example, live there.

Right in the south, many small islands line up in a long chain, the **Florida Keys**. A road with many bridges links them as far as **Key West**. Key West is the southernmost city of the 48 contiguous states of the USA. Around the islands lie coral reefs.

The capital is **Tallahassee** in the north-west. **Miami** is much better known, but it is not the seat of government. In 1513 the Spaniard Juan Ponce de León reached the coast and gave the land its name, which recalls flowers. Later Florida belonged to Spain for a long time. Since 1845 it has been a state of the USA.

On the east coast lies **Cape Canaveral**. There and on the neighbouring Merritt Island lie launch sites such as NASA’s **Kennedy Space Center**. From here the **Apollo missions** to the Moon were launched. Rockets still lift off there regularly today.

Florida has the nickname **“Sunshine State”** because the sun often shines there. It is warm all year round. That is why many tourists travel there. In late summer and autumn, however, strong tropical storms, the **hurricanes**, can pass over the land. “Golden State”, by the way, is the nickname of California.

gewusst: A great many oranges are grown in Florida.
In the waters of Florida live sea cows that are called manatees.

teile.einleitung: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels. They formed millions of years ago from the remains of plants and tiny living things, and to this day they supply a large part of the world’s energy.
wichtigste: Fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas.
They formed over millions of years from dead plants and tiny organisms.
They contain a lot of carbon.
When they are burned, the gas CO2 is produced.
Burning fossil fuels is the largest source of the extra CO2 in the air.
Fossil energy does not grow back, and the supplies are limited.

abschnitte.text: **Coal** formed mainly from the plants of huge swamp forests. The plants were covered by mud and rock and, over a very long time, transformed by pressure and heat. **Oil** and **natural gas** mostly formed from tiny living things in the sea, the **plankton**. Because they come from primeval times, they are called **fossil**. The word comes from the Latin word for “dug up”.

Fossil fuels supply heat, electricity and propulsion. Many houses are heated with **heating oil** and **natural gas**, in Switzerland too. **Petrol** and **diesel** from oil power cars, lorries and ships. In many countries, coal power stations produce electricity. **Plastics** are also made from oil.

Fossil fuels contain **carbon** that plants took up millions of years ago. When burned, it combines with oxygen to form **carbon dioxide (CO2)**. This gas enters the atmosphere. The burning of coal, oil and natural gas is the **largest source of the extra CO2** in the air. More CO2 strengthens the **greenhouse effect** and warms the Earth.

Fossil energy is **not renewable**. What we burn today took millions of years to form and does not grow back. Many countries therefore want to use more **renewable energy**, for example from sun, wind and water. Switzerland has set itself the goal of emitting no net greenhouse gases by 2050.

gewusst: With the steam engine, the great age of coal began in the 18th century.
Switzerland has hardly any fossil reserves of its own and imports almost all its oil and natural gas.

teile.einleitung: The Front Range is the easternmost mountain chain of the Rocky Mountains in the US state of Colorado. It rises almost abruptly out of the flat prairie.
wichtigste: The Front Range belongs to the Rocky Mountains.
It lies mainly in the state of Colorado.
To the east of it begin the flat Great Plains.
At its foot lie cities such as Denver and Boulder.
Several peaks are over 4,000 metres high.

abschnitte.text: Anyone travelling from the east through the flat **Great Plains** sees the **Front Range** as the first mountain chain of the **Rocky Mountains**. The name means roughly the “front chain”. Here the mountains rise directly out of the plain without a long stretch of hill country. Several peaks are over **4,000 metres** high, for example **Longs Peak** and **Pikes Peak**. Parts of the chain form the watershed between the Atlantic and the Pacific.

abschnitte.titel: Cities at the foot of the mountains
abschnitte.text: Along the foot of the mountains lie the large cities of Colorado. They include **Denver**, the capital of the state, and **Boulder**. Denver lies about one mile, that is, around 1,600 metres, above sea level and is therefore called the “Mile High City”. Most people in Colorado live in this strip at the edge of the mountains.

In the north of the Front Range lies **Rocky Mountain National Park**. There are forests, mountain lakes and high peaks there. Many people hike, climb or ski there. In the forests live animals such as **elk**, a large species of deer. In winter there is a lot of snow at the heights.

gewusst: From Pikes Peak, a teacher is said to have been inspired to write one of the best-known patriotic songs of the USA, “America the Beautiful”.

teile.einleitung: El Alto is a large city in Bolivia in South America. It lies at about 4,000 metres above sea level directly above La Paz and is among the highest large cities in the world.
wichtigste: El Alto lies in Bolivia on the high plain of the **Altiplano**.
The city lies at about 4,000 metres above sea level.
It lies directly above the basin of La Paz.
El Alto has grown very fast, mainly through people moving in from the countryside.
The international airport of La Paz is here.
Many residents belong to the **Aymara** people.

abschnitte.text: The **Altiplano** is a huge high plain in the Andes. El Alto lies right on the edge of this plain, where the land drops steeply into the basin of La Paz. The name means “the heights” in Spanish. At this height the air is thin, and even in summer it can get very cold at night. Anyone who has just arrived often feels **altitude sickness**, with headache and shortness of breath.

In the past, El Alto was only a suburb of La Paz. Many people moved here from villages in the countryside because they were looking for work. In this way El Alto grew quickly and in the 1980s became a city in its own right. Today very many people live here, and the city is one of the largest in Bolivia. Besides Spanish, many families also speak **Aymara**, an old language of the Andes.

Because there is no room in the narrow valley of La Paz, the airport lies up in El Alto. It is among the highest international airports in the world. Since 2014 a large network of **cable cars** has linked El Alto with La Paz. For many commuters this is faster than the bus on the winding roads.

In El Alto a huge street market takes place, where you can buy almost anything. Also well known are colourful buildings with playful façades, called **cholets**. They show how self-confident Aymara culture is in the city.

gewusst: The cable cars between La Paz and El Alto form one of the largest cable car networks in the world, used like a metro.
El Alto lies higher than the summit of the Titlis in central Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Yellow River, called Huang He in Chinese, is the second longest river in China. On its banks the first Chinese kingdoms arose, but its floods were always feared too.
wichtigste: The Yellow River is the second longest river in China after the Yangtze.
It is about 5,400 kilometres long and rises in the highlands of Tibet.
Its yellow colour comes from loess, a fine soil that it carries with it.
It runs into the Bohai Sea, part of the Yellow Sea.
Because of severe floods it is called “China’s Sorrow”.
The area along the river is regarded as the cradle of Chinese culture.

abschnitte.text: The **Yellow River** rises in the highlands of Tibet in Qinghai Province. From there it flows in a great arc to the north and then to the east through the north of China. It is about 5,400 kilometres long and so, after the **Yangtze**, the second longest river in the country. Finally it runs into the **Bohai Sea**. Many millions of people use its water for fields, cities and factories.

On its way the river flows through the **Loess Plateau**. **Loess** is a very fine, yellowish soil that the wind deposited long ago. Rain washes it away easily, and the river carries off huge amounts of it. That is why the water is murky and yellowish. The Yellow River is among the rivers with the most mud in the world.

The great amount of mud is deposited in the flat lower course and raises the river bed. People therefore built ever higher **dykes**. When a dyke broke, the water flooded wide areas. In the course of history the river shifted its course strongly several times, and at times the mouth lay far from where it is today. Because of these disasters it was given the nickname **“China’s Sorrow”**. Today reservoirs and dykes are meant to tame the floods.

On the middle and lower course the soil was fertile and easy to farm. Already thousands of years ago, farmers who grew millet lived there. Here the first **Chinese kingdoms** arose, for example the Shang dynasty. Important old capitals such as Xi’an and Luoyang lie near the river or its tributaries. That is why the Chinese often call the Yellow River their **mother river**.

gewusst: Because the river brings so much mud into the sea, its delta grows out into the sea year after year.
The Yellow Sea also gets its name from the colour of the mud that the rivers carry into it.

teile.einleitung: On 12 January 2010 a severe earthquake struck the Caribbean state of **Haiti**. It destroyed large parts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and was one of the deadliest quakes in history.
wichtigste: The quake had a **magnitude of 7.0**.
The epicentre lay near **Léogâne**, about 25 km from Port-au-Prince.
The focus lay only about **13 km** deep.
Haiti lies on the boundary between the **Caribbean** and **North American plates**.
About **1.5 million** people were made homeless.
The **National Palace** largely collapsed.
In October 2010 **cholera** broke out.

abschnitte.text: Haiti lies on the island of **Hispaniola** between two tectonic plates. The **Caribbean Plate** moves eastwards relative to the **North American Plate** at about 2 cm a year. In the south of Haiti runs the **Enriquillo-Plantain Garden Fault**, a so-called strike-slip fault, where rock slides sideways past each other. Later studies showed that mainly hidden side faults broke.

With a magnitude of **7.0**, the quake was only of medium strength. Even so, the damage was huge. The focus was very **shallow**, only about 13 km deep, and the epicentre only about 25 km from the densely populated capital. Many houses had been built without **earthquake protection** and collapsed. Besides the **National Palace**, the cathedral and many ministries were destroyed.

A year after the quake, the government of Haiti spoke of about **316,000** dead. Other estimates are lower, and the exact number is uncertain to this day. About **1.5 million** people lost their homes, and many lived in tent camps for a long time. In total about a third of the population was affected.

At that time the UN stabilisation mission **MINUSTAH** was operating in Haiti. Its headquarters collapsed, and its head, **Hédi Annabi**, lost his life, along with about 100 UN staff. Many countries, including Switzerland, sent helpers, money and material. The reconstruction took many years and is still difficult today in one of the poorest countries in the Americas.

In October 2010, **cholera** broke out in the weakened country, a disease that spreads through polluted water. It began in the Artibonite region and spread quickly. The germ had probably been brought in by UN peacekeeping soldiers. In 2016 the **UN** admitted a share of the responsibility.

gewusst: A quake of medium strength can be worse than a much stronger one if it is shallow and hits a big city with unsafe houses.
Haiti and the Dominican Republic share the island of Hispaniola, which the 2010 earthquake hit mainly in the Haitian part.

teile.einleitung: The Earth’s axis is an imaginary line through the North Pole and the South Pole, around which the Earth turns. It is tilted, and this is exactly the reason for the seasons.
wichtigste: The Earth’s axis is tilted by about **23.4 degrees**.
This angle is also called the **obliquity of the ecliptic**.
During a year, the axis almost always points in the same direction in space.
The tilt varies over about 41,000 years between about 22 and 24.5 degrees.
The slow spinning-top movement of the axis is called **precession**.
One precession cycle lasts about 26,000 years.
The position of the **polar circles** follows from the tilt.

abschnitte.text: The Earth circles the Sun and in doing so turns once a day on its **axis**. This axis is not perpendicular to the Earth’s orbit but is tilted by about **23.4 degrees**. Experts call this angle the **obliquity of the ecliptic**. Throughout a whole year the axis points almost unchanged in the same direction in space, roughly towards the **Pole Star**.

Because the axis always stays tilted the same way, in June the **northern hemisphere** is tilted towards the Sun. The Sun is then high in the sky for us, the days are long, and it is summer. In December the **southern hemisphere** is tilted towards the Sun, and for us it is winter. If the axis were not tilted, there would hardly be any seasons.

abschnitte.titel: Polar circles and the midnight sun
abschnitte.text: If you subtract the axial tilt from 90 degrees, you get the position of the **polar circles** at about 66.6 degrees north and south. North of the Arctic Circle, in midsummer the Sun does not set for at least one day. You can even see it at midnight, which is the **midnight sun**. In winter, conversely, there are days there when the Sun does not rise at all.

abschnitte.titel: The Earth’s axis as a spinning top
abschnitte.text: The Earth’s axis moves very slowly like a tilted **spinning top** and in doing so traces a cone. This movement is called **precession** and is caused mainly by the pull of the Sun and the Moon. One full cycle lasts about 25,800 years. As a result, the axis gradually points at other stars. In about 12,000 years the bright **Vega** in the constellation Lyra will stand near the celestial north pole.

The angle of tilt itself does not stay the same for ever either. It swings back and forth over about **41,000 years** between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees. At present the tilt is slowly decreasing. Such long swings influence how much sunlight the polar regions receive and play a part in the formation of **ice ages**.

gewusst: The Pole Star is our north star for only a few thousand years, and because of precession other stars take over this role later.
The tropics lie exactly at the latitude that corresponds to the axial tilt, that is, at about 23.4 degrees north and south.

teile.einleitung: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current in the Atlantic. Together with its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, it brings warm water as far as Europe and makes the climate there milder.
wichtigste: The warm Gulf Stream comes from the Gulf of Mexico.
Its continuation towards Europe is called the North Atlantic Current.
Together they make the climate in north-western Europe milder.
The Gulf Stream is part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
Juan Ponce de León was one of the first to describe the current off Florida in 1513.
Around 1770 Benjamin Franklin had one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream printed.

abschnitte.text: The **Gulf Stream** takes its name from the **Gulf of Mexico**, the region the warm water comes from. It flows through the Straits of Florida and then north along the east coast of North America. Later it turns east and crosses the Atlantic. This continuation towards Europe is called the **North Atlantic Current**. The Gulf Stream is one of the strongest ocean currents in the world.

The Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current carry huge amounts of heat. As a result, the climate in **north-western Europe** is **milder** than it would otherwise be so far north. The ports in the north of **Norway** usually stay **free of ice** even in winter. Even **Murmansk** in Russia, north of the Arctic Circle, is free of ice all year round thanks to branches of the North Atlantic Current. Switzerland also benefits indirectly from the mild westerly winds.

The Gulf Stream is part of the **Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation**. The warm water flows north at the surface. There it cools, becomes saltier and heavier and sinks into the depths. In the depths it then flows slowly south again. This creates a huge conveyor belt. Researchers are investigating whether this conveyor belt is weakening because of **climate change**.

The Spanish navigator **Juan Ponce de León** was one of the first to describe the strong current off **Florida** in 1513. His ships barely made any headway despite a following wind. Around 1770 the American statesman **Benjamin Franklin** had one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream printed. He wanted to make sure that mail ships between America and England reached their destination faster.

Ocean currents are often measured in a unit called the **sverdrup**. One sverdrup is equal to **one million cubic metres** of water per second. The unit is named after the Norwegian oceanographer Harald Sverdrup. The Gulf Stream carries many sverdrups, far more water than all the rivers on Earth put together.

gewusst: All the rivers in the world together bring roughly one sverdrup of water into the sea.
Because the Gulf Stream is so warm, it is easy to recognise on satellite images of sea temperature.

teile.einleitung: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world. With its long neck it eats leaves high up in the trees of the African savannah.
wichtigste: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world.
Its long tongue is dark to bluish.
On its head it has small horns covered in fur.
Every coat pattern is different, like a fingerprint.
To drink, it spreads its front legs.
A baby giraffe is about 1.8 metres tall at birth and falls almost 2 metres.

abschnitte.text: The **giraffe** lives in the savannahs of **Africa**. Fully grown animals can be over five metres tall, which makes it the **tallest animal in the world**. Its neck is very long, but like ours it has only **seven neck bones**. They are simply much bigger. Its heart is also very strong, so that the blood is pumped all the way up into the head.

Giraffes eat mainly leaves, especially from **acacia trees**. With their long, flexible **tongue** they pluck the leaves from between the thorns. The tongue is **dark to bluish**, and the dark colour probably protects it from sunburn. To drink, the giraffe has to **spread its front legs** and bend its head far down. In this position it is vulnerable, so it drinks only briefly.

On its head the giraffe has small **horns covered in fur**. They are called **ossicones**. They are made of bone and covered with skin and fur. The brown spotted **coat** is different on every giraffe, and no pattern is the same as another. Researchers can therefore recognise giraffes by their coat pattern, rather like people by their fingerprints.

Giraffe mothers give birth to their young **standing up**. The young one **falls** almost **2 metres** to the ground. That sounds dangerous, but it does not harm it. A **baby giraffe** is already about **1.8 metres** tall at birth. After a short time it stands on its wobbly legs and soon can run along with its mother.

Adult giraffes have few enemies, mainly lions. With their strong legs, though, they can defend themselves well. Life is more dangerous for the young animals. Today giraffes have become rarer in many places because their habitat is getting smaller. Many nature reserves in Africa help to protect them.

gewusst: Giraffes sleep very little, often only for short stretches at a time.
A giraffe’s tongue can be about half a metre long.

teile.einleitung: An effective climate classification sorts the climates of the Earth by measurable values such as temperature and precipitation. The best known is the Köppen-Geiger classification. With short letter formulas such as Cfb or BWh, it describes the climate of a place.
wichtigste: The best-known effective climate classification goes back to Wladimir Köppen.
Rudolf Geiger later revised it with him.
The main letters A to E stand for large climate zones, and B for dry climates.
In A climates, the coldest month is on average at least 18 °C.
Small letters show when it rains: “f” means moist all year round, “s” a dry summer.
The Swiss Plateau has a Cfb climate.

abschnitte.text: A climate classification divides the Earth into climate regions. It is called **effective** when it sorts climates by **measurable values** and their **effects**, for example on the plant world. So you look at temperature and precipitation and at which vegetation can grow there. Other, so-called genetic classifications, by contrast, sort climates by their causes, for example by air currents.

The classification most widely used in the world today was developed by the climatologist **Wladimir Köppen** around 1900. He took strong guidance from the boundaries of the great vegetation zones. Later he revised it together with **Rudolf Geiger**, which is why it is called the **Köppen-Geiger classification**. It is still used in textbooks and in research today.

Five capital letters stand for the main climates. **A** are tropical climates: the **coldest month** is on average **at least 18 °C**. **B** stands for **dry climates**, in which more water could evaporate than falls as rain. **C** are warm temperate climates and **D** cold, snowy climates. In Köppen’s original version, a coldest month of **minus 3 °C** separates the C from the D climates. **E** are the polar climates.

Further letters refine the formula. The **“f”** means that it is **moist all year round**, as in the tropical rainforest climate **Af**. An **“s”** means that the **summer is dry**, for example in the Mediterranean climate **Csa**. A **“w”** stands for dry winters. Among the dry climates, **BWh** means a **hot desert climate**, for example in the Sahara. Among the polar climates, **ET** is the tundra climate. In the ice climate **EF**, even the **warmest month is below 0 °C**.

The **Swiss Plateau**, for example Zurich, has a **Cfb climate** according to Köppen-Geiger. The C stands for warm temperate, the f for precipitation in all seasons, and the b for a warm but not hot summer. In the higher parts of the Alps, by contrast, there are cooler climate types, and on the highest peaks even polar climate. In this way the formula shows at a glance how climates differ.

gewusst: Köppen also worked as a botanist. That is why plants play such a big part in his classification.
With the Köppen-Geiger classification, researchers also show how climate zones shift because of warming.

teile.einleitung: The demographic transition model describes how the population of a country changes as it develops. Birth and death rates fall from high to low values. In between, the population often grows strongly.
wichtigste: The model describes the change from high to low birth and death rates.
In the first stage, birth and death rates are high.
In the early transitional stage, the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high.
In the third stage, the birth rate begins to fall markedly.
The difference between the birth rate and the death rate is called the natural growth rate.
Frank W. Notestein developed the model decisively further in 1945.
Critics say it is based mainly on European countries.

abschnitte.text: The **birth rate** shows how many children are born per year per 1,000 inhabitants. The **death rate** shows how many people die per 1,000 inhabitants. The difference between the two is called the **natural growth rate**. The **demographic transition** model shows how these rates change as a country develops. The American demographer **Frank W. Notestein** developed it decisively further in 1945.

In the first, **pre-transitional** stage, **birth and death rates are high**. There are many children, but many people also die young, for example of disease or hunger. The population hardly grows. In the second, **early transitional** stage, nutrition, hygiene and medicine improve. The **death rate falls** while the birth rate stays high. As a result, the population grows especially strongly.

In the third, **mid-transitional** stage, the **birth rate begins to fall markedly**. The reasons include better education, work in cities and pension schemes. Later, both rates are low, and the population grows only slowly. Countries such as Switzerland are in this late stage.

Some models describe a **fifth stage**. In it the **death rate is higher than the birth rate**, because there are many older people. Without immigration, the population then shrinks. Japan and Italy are examples of countries with this development.

With the **rule of 70** you can estimate when a population will double: you divide 70 by the annual growth rate in per cent. At 2 per cent growth, this comes to about **35 years**. A common criticism of the model is that it is based mainly on the development of **European countries**. Other countries go through the stages partly faster or in a different way.

gewusst: The rule of 70 also works for money: at 7 per cent interest, an amount doubles in about 10 years.
Europe took over a hundred years to go through the demographic transition, and some countries in Asia much less.

teile.einleitung: The Deccan is a large plateau in the south of India. It takes up a large part of the Indian peninsula. The name comes from an old word for “south”.
wichtigste: The Deccan lies in the south of the Indian peninsula.
It is bounded in the west by the Western Ghats and in the east by the Eastern Ghats.
The Deccan Traps in the north-west are made of basalt.
Most of the big rivers, such as the Godavari and the Krishna, flow east.
Bangalore, on the Deccan, is a centre of the Indian IT industry.
The dark black soil (regur) is well suited to cotton.

abschnitte.text: The **Deccan** is a plateau in the **south** of the Indian peninsula, which is shaped like a triangle. In the west it is bounded by the **Western Ghats**, a mountain range along the coast. In the east lie the lower **Eastern Ghats**. The name comes from the Sanskrit word “dakshina”, which means “south”.

In the north-west, the Deccan consists of huge layers of **basalt**, a dark volcanic rock. These **Deccan Traps** formed about 66 million years ago. At that time a huge amount of lava flowed over a long period from cracks in the Earth. In places the layers are over a thousand metres thick and look like steps, hence the name trap, from the Swedish word for staircase.

Because the plateau slopes down to the east, most of the big rivers flow **east** into the Bay of Bengal. They include the **Godavari**, the **Krishna** and the Kaveri. At their mouths there are fertile deltas where a lot of rice is grown. The monsoon rain in summer is very important for farming.

The weathered basalt produced a dark, fertile soil, the **black soil** or **regur**. It can store a lot of water. For this reason it is especially well suited to growing **cotton**. It is therefore also called cotton soil.

Large cities lie on the Deccan. **Bangalore**, now officially Bengaluru, is known as the centre of the Indian **IT industry**. Many companies there develop software for the whole world. Hyderabad also lies on the plateau and is an important location for technology.

gewusst: The huge lava eruptions of the Deccan Traps fell at the same time that the dinosaurs died out.
Bangalore is often called the “Silicon Valley of India”.

teile.einleitung: A diaspora is a group of people who live outside their country of origin and nevertheless feel connected to it. Many peoples have a diaspora, often as a result of hardship, persecution or emigration. Switzerland, too, has a large community abroad, the “Fifth Switzerland”.
wichtigste: The Greek word “diaspora” literally means dispersion.
Originally it meant the Jews who lived outside the land of Israel.
The great famine from 1845 drove very many people to emigrate from Ireland.
The Armenian diaspora is clearly larger than the population of Armenia.
The African diaspora in the Americas is above all a result of the slave trade.
At the end of 2024, over 800,000 Swiss people lived abroad, most of them in France.

abschnitte.text: The word **diaspora** comes from Greek and means **dispersion**. At first it was used for the **Jewish communities** that lived outside the land of Israel. Even in ancient times many Jews were deported or emigrated, for example to Babylon, Egypt or Rome. For centuries they kept their religion, their festivals and their traditions in foreign lands. Today the term is used for many different peoples.

A diaspora often arises through great hardship. From **1845**, a potato disease destroyed the most important food in **Ireland**. In the **Great Famine**, very many people died, and hundreds of thousands emigrated to America. Today a large share of the **Armenians** live outside Armenia, partly as a result of the genocide in the Ottoman Empire from 1915. Their diaspora is clearly larger than the population of their own state.

Millions of people of African origin live in North and South America and in the Caribbean. Their ancestors were forcibly taken from Africa above all through the **transatlantic slave trade**. This history shapes the societies concerned to this day. At the same time, the African diaspora has strongly influenced music, language, religion and cooking in the Americas, for example with jazz, blues and samba.

The Swiss abroad are often called the **Fifth Switzerland**, in addition to the four language regions. According to statistics, at the end of 2024 **over 800,000** Swiss citizens lived abroad. Most live in **France**, followed by Germany, the USA and Italy, among others. Swiss citizens abroad may take part in federal votes and elections. In the 19th century many people emigrated from Switzerland because of poverty, for example to America.

Many people in a diaspora keep close ties both to their **country of origin** and to their new country of residence. Experts speak of **transnationalism**. People phone their families, send money home, travel back on holiday and celebrate the festivals of both countries. With the internet it has become much easier to keep such connections over great distances.

gewusst: In the US state of Wisconsin there is the town of New Glarus, founded in 1845 by emigrants from the canton of Glarus.
In Brazil lies the town of Nova Friburgo, founded by emigrants from the canton of Fribourg.

teile.einleitung: A flag is a piece of cloth with colours and signs that stands for a country, a region or a community. Every country in the world has its own national flag. The Swiss flag with the white cross on red is recognised all over the world.
wichtigste: A flag is a mark of recognition made of cloth with colours and symbols.
The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background.
The Swiss flag is square, like that of the Vatican, and no other.
Japan’s flag is white with a red circle that represents the Sun.
The flag of the USA has 50 stars, one for each state.
The study of flags is called vexillology.
Every Swiss canton has its own flag.

abschnitte.text: A **flag** is a usually rectangular cloth that is fixed to a mast or a pole. It shows colours, stripes, crosses, stars or coats of arms. Flags show which country, club or organisation something belongs to. In the past, they were used in war or at sea to recognise who was friend and who was foe.

The Swiss flag shows a free-standing **white cross on a red background**. It is **square**, which is a special feature that it shares only with the flag of the Vatican. On ships a rectangular version is used. The emblem goes back to the banner of the canton of Schwyz, after which Switzerland is also named.

The flag of **Japan** is white with a red circle in the middle that represents the rising Sun. The flag of the **USA** has 50 stars for the 50 states and 13 stripes for the 13 founding colonies. France has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red. The flag of Nepal is the only national flag that is not rectangular, and it consists of two triangles one above the other.

The colours of a flag often have a meaning. Green often stands for nature or Islam, and red for courage or the blood of freedom fighters. Many Scandinavian countries such as Denmark, Sweden and Norway have a horizontal cross, the so-called **Scandinavian cross**. The flag of Denmark is regarded as one of the oldest national flags still in use.

Not only countries have flags. The **Red Cross** was founded in Geneva in 1863, and its emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed. The Olympic flag shows five interlocking rings on a white background. The European Union and the UN also have flags of their own.

The science that studies flags is called **vexillology**. The word comes from the Latin vexillum, which means banner. Flags are raised on special occasions, for example on 1 August, the Swiss national day. In mourning a flag is flown at **half-mast**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of flags.
A flag that is raised only halfway, as a sign of mourning.
The official flag of a country.
To pull a flag up a mast.

gewusst: The flag of Nepal is the only national flag in the world that is not four-sided.
The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed, as an honour to Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Drake Passage is the stretch of sea between the southern tip of South America and Antarctica. It links the Atlantic with the Pacific. Because of its high waves and storms, it is regarded as one of the roughest seas in the world.
wichtigste: The Drake Passage lies between Cape Horn and the Antarctic Peninsula.
It links the Atlantic and the Pacific Ocean.
At its narrowest point it is about 800 kilometres wide.
It is named after the English seafarer Francis Drake.
Strong storms and very high waves are common here.

abschnitte.text: The **Drake Passage** separates **Cape Horn**, the southern tip of South America, from the **Antarctic Peninsula**. It is the shortest link between Antarctica and another continent. It is named after the English seafarer **Francis Drake**, who sailed round the world in the 16th century. In Spanish-speaking countries it is also named after the Spanish seafarer Francisco de Hoces.

In the Drake Passage there is no land to slow the wind and the waves. Here flows the **Antarctic Circumpolar Current**, a mighty ocean current that runs right round Antarctica. For this reason violent **storms** often rage, and the waves can be many metres high. In the past, sailors greatly feared rounding Cape Horn. Today expedition ships cross the Drake Passage on their way to Antarctica, which usually takes about two days.

The cold, nutrient-rich water is full of life. There is plenty of **krill** here, small crustaceans that serve as food for many other animals. Whales, seals, penguins and albatrosses can be seen in the area. The Drake Passage is therefore also very exciting for researchers.

gewusst: Because the crossing is often very stormy, travellers speak of the “Drake Shake” when the ship rocks especially hard.

teile.einleitung: Not every desert consists of sand. A **rock desert** is a dry landscape of bare rock and boulders. Large parts of the Sahara are rock deserts of this kind.
wichtigste: A rock desert consists mainly of bare rock and boulders.
In the Sahara, a rock desert is called by an Arabic technical word, **hamada**.
Large temperature differences between day and night make the rocks split.
The wind blows away fine sand, and the rock is left behind.
Besides rock deserts there are gravel deserts and sand deserts.

abschnitte.text: Many people think of high sand dunes when they think of a desert. But sand deserts make up only part of the deserts. Large areas are **rock deserts** of bare rock, slabs of stone and boulders. In the Sahara they are called by an Arabic word, **hamada**. There are also **gravel deserts** of small stones and **sand deserts**, which are called an **erg**.

In the desert it gets very hot during the day, but at night it can cool down strongly. In heat the rock expands, and in cold it contracts. Through these large **temperature differences**, cracks form over time, and the rocks **split**. This is called **weathering**. Over a very long time the fragments turn into gravel and sand. The **wind** carries off fine sand, so in many places bare rock is left behind.

Rock deserts look empty, but there is life there. Lizards, scorpions and insects hide in the shade of the stones during the day. Plants grow in crevices where a little water collects after rare rainfalls. For people, rock deserts are hard to cross, because the terrain is stony and uneven.

gewusst: On rocks in the Sahara, ancient rock paintings are found that show animals such as giraffes, from when the area was still green.

teile.einleitung: A geographic information system, GIS for short, is a computer program that links data to a place on Earth and shows it on maps. With it you can show, for example, where roads, houses, forests or bus stops are, and analyse this information. Navigation apps, weather maps and planning offices all work with GIS.
wichtigste: A GIS stores, manages, analyses and displays data with a location.
Roads as lines and buildings as areas are mostly stored as vector data.
Georeferencing means assigning spatial coordinates to data.
The current national coordinate system of Switzerland is called LV95.
In Switzerland the federal office swisstopo is responsible for national surveying and official maps.
In a buffer analysis, a zone at a fixed distance around an object is calculated.
Roger Tomlinson is regarded as the father of geographic information systems.

abschnitte.text: A **geographic information system** connects information with a place on Earth. It can store, edit, analyse and display such data as a map. The data are laid on top of each other in **layers**, like transparent sheets, for example one layer for roads, one for rivers and one for houses. In this way you can recognise connections that stay invisible in a single list.

A GIS knows two main kinds of data. **Vector data** consist of points, lines and areas, for example a bus stop as a point, a road as a line and a building as an area. **Raster data** consist of many small squares, the pixels, as in an aerial photograph or satellite image. Each pixel can store a value, such as the height or the temperature.

So that a computer knows where something lies, every piece of information needs **coordinates**, which is called **georeferencing**. Switzerland today uses the national coordinate system **LV95**, whose values are given in metres. For national surveying and the official maps, the federal office **swisstopo** in Wabern near Bern is responsible. On a map at a scale of 1:25,000, 4 centimetres on the map correspond to 1,000 metres in nature.

With a GIS you can answer questions, for example: which houses lie less than 300 metres from a stop? For this you do a **buffer analysis**, that is, a zone at a fixed distance around an object. You can also overlay layers, for example to find areas that are at the same time flat, sunny and not in a forest. The fastest route from A to B is also calculated in this way.

In the 1960s the geographer **Roger Tomlinson** developed the first large geographic information system in Canada to record areas of land. He is therefore regarded as the father of geographic information systems. With faster computers, satellites and **GPS**, GIS became ever more widespread from the 1990s. Today almost everyone with a smartphone carries a small GIS application in their pocket.

Navigation apps use geodata to calculate the best route. Ambulance services and the fire brigade use them to find the scene quickly. Local authorities plan new districts, routes to school or cycle paths with GIS. On the federal map portal, anyone can look at Swiss maps, aerial photographs and hiking trails free of charge.

begriffe.erklaerung: Information that is linked to a place on Earth.
Data made of points, lines and areas.
Data made of many small squares, as in a photo.
Data are assigned coordinates so that you know where they lie.
Says how much a map is reduced compared with reality.

gewusst: In the Swiss coordinate system LV95, the easting values begin with a 2 and the northing values with a 1, so that you do not mix them up.
Swisstopo regularly makes aerial photographs of the whole of Switzerland from aeroplanes.

teile.einleitung: After the Volga, the Danube is the second longest river in Europe. It rises in the Black Forest in Germany and flows about 2,850 kilometres to the Black Sea. On the way it crosses ten countries and four capital cities, more than any other river in the world.
wichtigste: The Danube rises in the Black Forest.
It flows into the Black Sea.
The Danube flows through 10 countries.
Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade lie on the Danube, but Prague does not.
The Inn from the Engadine brings water from Switzerland into the Danube.
At about 2,850 kilometres, it is the second longest river in Europe.
The Danube Delta is a huge nature reserve.

abschnitte.text: The Danube begins in the **Black Forest** in the south-west of Germany. At Donaueschingen the two source rivers **Brigach and Breg** join. From there the Danube flows east, that is, in the opposite direction to the Rhine. On its way it crosses Bavaria and reaches Austria at Passau.

The Danube flows through or along ten countries: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine. No other river in the world touches so many states. On it lie the four **capital cities** of Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. Prague does not lie on the Danube but on the Vltava.

The **Inn** rises in the Engadine in the canton of Graubünden. It flows through Austria and joins the Danube at Passau. There the Inn often even carries more water than the Danube itself. In this way water from the Swiss Alps reaches the Black Sea.

Shortly before the **Black Sea**, the Danube splits into many arms and forms a large **delta**. It lies mainly in Romania and in small part in Ukraine. The Danube Delta is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site. Pelicans, many other water birds and numerous species of fish live there.

Since Roman times the Danube has been an important **transport route**, and for a long time it formed the border of the Roman Empire. Today cargo ships and river cruise ships travel on it. Through the Main-Danube Canal it is linked to the Rhine and so to the North Sea. Many power stations on the Danube produce electricity from hydropower.

In Budapest, the magnificent Parliament building and famous bridges stand right on the bank. In Austria, the **Wachau** valley with its vineyards and castles is well known. The composer Johann Strauss wrote the famous waltz “On the Beautiful Blue Danube”. At the Iron Gates between Serbia and Romania, the river squeezes through a narrow gorge.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where a river begins.
The place where a river flows into a sea, a lake or another river.
A river mouth area in which a river divides into many arms.
A river that flows into a larger river, like the Inn into the Danube.

gewusst: At the Danube Sinkhole near Immendingen, the young Danube seeps entirely into the ground on some days, and part of the water flows underground to the Rhine.
The Danube flows through more capital cities than any other river on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A mountain range is a large group of mountains that are joined together and often stretch for hundreds or thousands of kilometres. Most mountain ranges formed because huge plates of the Earth’s crust were pushed against each other. Mountains shape the climate, the rivers and the lives of people.
wichtigste: A mountain range consists of many joined mountains and valleys.
The Urals are regarded as the border between Europe and Asia.
The Pyrenees form the border between France and Spain.
The Rocky Mountains stretch across the west of North America from Canada to the USA.
