The Atlas Mountains lie in the north-west of Africa, mainly in Morocco.
The Himalayas are the highest mountains, and the Andes the longest range on land.
The Alps and the Jura are the mountains of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **mountain range** is a large area with many mountains, peaks, valleys and passes. A long row of mountains is called a **mountain chain**. Mountain ranges can be a few hundred metres or over 8,000 metres high. There are also huge mountain ranges on the sea floor, the mid-ocean ridges.

Most large mountain ranges are **fold mountains**. They form when two plates of the Earth collide and the rock is pushed together, folded and forced upwards. This is how the Alps formed, when the African Plate pressed against the Eurasian Plate. Other mountains, such as parts of the Andes, are shaped by volcanoes. Old mountain ranges such as the Urals have been worn down over millions of years and are therefore lower today.

The **Urals** in Russia are regarded as the border between Europe and Asia. The **Pyrenees** separate France and Spain, and in the middle lies the small state of Andorra. The **Rocky Mountains** stretch across the west of North America from Canada to the USA. The **Atlas Mountains** lie in the north-west of Africa, mainly in Morocco.

The **Himalayas** in Asia are the highest mountains on Earth, and Mount Everest stands there. The **Andes** in South America, at about 7,000 kilometres, are the longest mountain range on land. At about 1,200 kilometres long, the Alps are the largest mountain range that lies entirely in Europe. They stretch across eight countries, from France to Slovenia.

The **Alps** cover about 60 per cent of the area of Switzerland. In the north-west lies the **Jura**, a lower fold mountain range with rounded tops and limestone rock. Between the Alps and the Jura lies the Central Plateau, where most people live. Even a geological period is named after the Jura, the Jurassic, in which the dinosaurs lived.

In the mountains, climate and plants change with altitude, which is called **altitudinal zonation**. At the bottom grow deciduous forests, further up coniferous forests, above them Alpine pastures and finally only rock and ice. Animals such as the ibex, the chamois, the llama or the snow leopard are adapted to life in the mountains. Mountains are important water stores, for many large rivers rise there.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain range in which layers of rock were pushed together and folded.
A long row of joined mountains.
Zones with different plants, depending on the height above sea level.
A crossing over a mountain range at a low point between peaks.

gewusst: On some peaks of the Alps you can find fossilised shells, because the rock once lay on the sea floor.
The Alps are still slowly being uplifted today, while at the same time erosion wears them down.

teile.einleitung: Iron ore is a rock from which iron is obtained. Iron is the most important raw material for steel, from which bridges, cars, rails and machines are built. Today Australia mines the most iron ore.
wichtigste: Iron ore is rock that contains a lot of iron.
Australia mines the most iron ore (as of 2024).
Important iron ores are haematite and magnetite.
In the blast furnace, pig iron is obtained from iron ore.
Steel is made from pig iron.

abschnitte.text: Iron almost never occurs pure in nature. It is combined with oxygen and other substances and is found in certain rocks, the **iron ores**. The most important are **haematite**, which is often reddish, and **magnetite**, which is magnetic. Good iron ore contains a lot of iron. The largest deposits are very old and formed billions of years ago in the primeval oceans.

In 2024 **Australia** mined the most iron ore, mainly in the **Pilbara** region in the west of the country. **Brazil**, China and India also mine large amounts. The ore is often extracted in huge **open-cast mines**, that is, in open pits. Very long goods trains take it to the ports, and from there ships sail mainly to China. In Switzerland iron ore was also once mined, for example at the **Gonzen** near Sargans, but not any more today.

In the **blast furnace**, the ore is strongly heated together with **coke**, a kind of coal. This removes the oxygen from the iron, and liquid **pig iron** flows out. Pig iron still contains a lot of carbon and is brittle. In a further step it is turned into **steel**, which is strong and flexible. Today people are looking for ways to make steel with less carbon dioxide, for example with hydrogen.

gewusst: The red colour of Mars comes from iron oxide, that is, a kind of rust in the dust.
Steel is among the materials that are recycled most often.

teile.einleitung: The cheetah is the fastest land animal in the world. It lives mainly in the open savannas of Africa and hunts with short, lightning-fast sprints.
wichtigste: The cheetah can run at about 100 km/h, but only briefly.
It hunts best in the open savanna and mostly by day.
Its prey is often gazelles.
It has many black spots in its coat and black stripes on its face like tears.
Its long tail helps it not to fall over in bends.
The cheetah cannot roar, but purrs and chirps.

abschnitte.text: A **cheetah** can run at about **100 km/h** and reaches this speed in a few seconds. Its body is slim and light, and its legs are long. Its **spine** is very flexible, so it makes huge bounds. It cannot run so fast for long, though: after a short sprint it is exhausted and has to recover.

Cheetahs live mainly in **Africa**, in the open **savanna** with plenty of grass and few trees. There they can see their prey from far away and have room to run. A very small population still lives in Iran. Unlike lions or leopards, cheetahs mostly hunt **by day**. In this way they keep out of the way of the stronger predators that hunt at night.

The cheetah first creeps up on its prey. Then it starts a fast sprint. It often hunts **gazelles** and other smaller antelopes. When the prey doubles back, its long **tail** helps like a rudder so that it does not fall over in the bend. It can retract its claws only a little, and when running they grip the ground like spikes.

The coat of the cheetah is golden yellow with many small **black spots**. Typical are the two black stripes that run from the eyes to the mouth like **tears**. They are meant to keep off some of the dazzling sun. Cheetahs **cannot roar**. They **purr** like house cats and make high, chirping sounds that sound almost like bird calls.

Cheetahs are endangered. Their habitat is getting smaller because people use more and more land. In addition, their prey is often taken away from them again by lions and hyenas. Nature reserves and projects with farmers are meant to help protect the cheetahs. In some Swiss zoos you can see cheetahs.

gewusst: A cheetah can accelerate from zero to almost 100 km/h in about three seconds.
Young cheetahs have a long, pale mane on the back that makes them look like a honey badger.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is our home planet. It circles the Sun and is the only planet where we know that there is life.
wichtigste: The Earth is a **planet**.
It is the **third** planet from the Sun.
**Eight** planets circle our Sun.
The Earth is also called the “Blue Planet” because a lot of **water** covers it.
It needs **one year** for a round of the Sun.
In a leap year there is **29 February**.
**Jupiter** is much bigger than the Earth.

abschnitte.text: **Eight planets** circle our Sun. From the Sun, first come **Mercury** and **Venus**, then the **Earth** follows as the third planet. After that come Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mercury, Venus and Mars are smaller than the Earth. **Jupiter** is the largest planet in our solar system.

About **two thirds** of the Earth are covered with **oceans**. From space it therefore looks blue, and it is called the “Blue Planet”. White clouds drift across it, and there is ice at the poles. The Earth has an **envelope of air**, the atmosphere. It contains oxygen to breathe and protects us from dangerous radiation.

Plants, animals and people live on the Earth. To this day we know of no other planet on which there are **living things**. The Earth has exactly the right distance from the Sun: it is not too hot and not too cold, and there is liquid **water**. All living things need this.

The Earth turns once a day on itself. That is why there are **day and night**. At the same time it circles the Sun. For one round it needs about **365 days**, which is one year. Strictly speaking, it is a little more than 365 days. That is why almost every four years there is an extra day, **29 February**. Such a year is called a **leap year**.

The **Moon** circles the Earth. It is much smaller than the Earth and does not shine by itself but is lit by the Sun. For one round of the Earth it needs about a month. The Moon is the only heavenly body besides the Earth on which people have stood.

gewusst: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
Anyone born on 29 February can celebrate their birthday on the right day only in a leap year.

teile.einleitung: **Crude oil** is a dark, thick raw material from the ground. It is used to make petrol, heating oil and plastics, and for many countries it is the most important source of income.
wichtigste: Because of its colour and its value, crude oil is often called **black gold**.
A **barrel**, the usual unit for crude oil, holds about 159 litres.
On the Persian Gulf, oil was found for the first time in Iran in 1908.
In Saudi Arabia, large amounts of oil were first struck in 1938.
Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world (as of 2024).
The USA has produced the most oil since 2018 (as of 2024).
Because of the oil crisis of 1973, there were car-free Sundays in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Crude oil formed millions of years ago from tiny dead sea creatures. They sank to the seabed and were slowly transformed under layers of mud and rock. Today the oil is pumped from deep boreholes. It is measured in **barrels**, which are about 159 litres. Because it is so valuable, it is also called **black gold**.

On the Persian Gulf lie huge deposits. In 1908 oil was found for the first time in this region in **Iran**. In **Saudi Arabia** large amounts were struck in 1938. **Ghawar**, the largest conventional oil field in the world, is also there. Qatar and Iran share the largest **natural gas field** on Earth in the Gulf. Dubai, by contrast, has only small oil reserves and therefore relies strongly on **tourism** and **trade**.

The largest proven **reserves** are held by Venezuela (as of 2024). Reserves are the amounts that still lie in the ground and can be recovered. The most oil has been **produced** since 2018 in the USA (as of 2024). There a lot of oil is obtained from tight rock with new methods. Crude oil is a **fossil raw material**: when burned it produces carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change.

In 1973 several Arab producing countries cut back their deliveries, and the oil price rose sharply. This **oil crisis** also hit Switzerland, which has to import all its oil. In autumn 1973 the Federal Council ordered three **car-free Sundays**. Many people used the empty roads for cycling, walking or even roller skating. The crisis showed how dependent the country was on oil.

gewusst: Crude oil is used to make not only fuels but also plastics, paints and many medicines.
Switzerland has no oil of its own that is produced, and buys everything abroad.

teile.einleitung: A developing country is a country in which many people are poor and schools, hospitals or clean water are often lacking. Today people also often speak of the Global South or of low-income countries. To compare countries, experts use measures such as the Human Development Index.
wichtigste: Developing countries have a comparatively low income and often weaker provision of education and health.
The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education and income.
A Gini coefficient of 0 means that everyone has exactly the same income.
Purchasing power parity evens out price differences between countries.
The UN’s Agenda 2030 includes 17 goals for sustainable development.
The Brandt Report of 1980 shaped the idea of a north-south dividing line.
Dependency theory explains underdevelopment by dependence on the industrialised countries.

abschnitte.text: A **developing country** is a country in which a large part of the population has little money available. Often clean drinking water, electricity, good schools or hospitals are lacking. Many of these countries lie in Africa south of the Sahara, in parts of Asia and in Latin America. Countries that are developing quickly, such as Brazil or India, are called **emerging countries**.

The **gross domestic product (GDP)** per head shows how much economic output falls on average to one person. Example: a GDP of 720 billion francs divided by 9 million inhabitants gives 80,000 francs per head. Since a loaf of bread or a bus ride does not cost the same everywhere, figures are often converted using **purchasing power parity**. In this way price differences between countries are evened out.

Since 1990 the UN has calculated the **Human Development Index (HDI)**. It combines three areas: life expectancy, education and income. Switzerland regularly ranks among the leaders, while countries such as South Sudan or Somalia are far behind. The **Gini coefficient** measures how unequally income is distributed: 0 means complete equality, and 1 means that one person owns everything.

The **Brandt Report** of 1980, named after the former German chancellor Willy Brandt, drew a dividing line between the rich north and the poor south of the world. From this came the idea of the **north-south divide**. **Dependency theory** explains the poverty of many countries by their dependence on the industrialised countries, for example because they sell only cheap raw materials. Other explanations stress wars, corruption, climate or a lack of education.

In 2015 the member states of the UN adopted **Agenda 2030** with 17 goals for sustainable development. They include an end to poverty and hunger, good education, clean water and climate protection. The goals apply to all countries, including Switzerland. In English they are called the Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs for short.

Switzerland supports poorer countries through **development cooperation**. The main body responsible is the SDC, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation of the federal government. Aid organisations such as Helvetas, Caritas or the Swiss Red Cross are also involved. They help, for example, with building wells, with schools or in agriculture.

begriffe.erklaerung: The economic output of a country divided by the number of inhabitants.
A conversion that takes account of how much money can really buy in a country.
A UN value that combines life expectancy, education and income.
A number between 0 and 1 that shows how unequally income is distributed.
A country that is quickly developing from a developing country into an industrialised country.

gewusst: In the 1950s South Korea was one of the poorest countries in the world, and today it is among the rich industrialised countries.
Australia also lies in the southern hemisphere but still counts as part of the rich “north” of the Brandt Report.

teile.einleitung: A geyser is a hot spring that at intervals shoots a fountain of boiling water and steam into the air. Geysers exist in only a few places on Earth, where hot rock lies close below the surface.
wichtigste: A geyser is a spring that squirts hot water upwards.
Hot rock deep down heats the water, and steam pushes it upwards.
All geysers are named after the Geysir in Iceland.
The Strokkur in Iceland erupts every few minutes.
In Yellowstone National Park in the USA there are the most geysers in the world.
There also stand the famous Old Faithful and Steamboat Geyser, the highest active geyser.

abschnitte.text: Beneath a geyser lies a narrow channel that reaches deep into the ground and is filled with water. **Hot rock** in the depths heats this water strongly. Because the water above it presses down heavily, it can become hotter than 100 degrees at the bottom without boiling. At some point **steam** does form. The steam expands and hurls the water upwards with great force. After that the channel slowly fills up again, and everything begins anew.

The name comes from a famous **spring in Iceland** called **Geysir**. The Icelandic word means roughly “the one that gushes forth”. All such springs were later named after it. The Great Geysir in the valley of Haukadalur now erupts only rarely. Very close by, however, the **Strokkur** reliably shoots a fountain of water into the air every few minutes.

In **Yellowstone National Park** in the USA there are the most geysers in the world, more than half of all those known. The best known is **Old Faithful**. It erupts fairly regularly, so that the eruptions can be predicted quite well. **Steamboat Geyser** is the highest active geyser in the world. Its fountains can reach over 90 metres, but it erupts irregularly.

You must not get too close to a geyser. The water is **boiling hot** and can cause severe burns. The ground around hot springs is also often thin and can give way. That is why there are boardwalks and barriers in national parks. Anyone who stays on the paths can marvel at the eruptions safely.

gewusst: Geysers exist in only a few places, for example in Iceland, the USA, New Zealand, Chile and on the Russian peninsula of Kamchatka.
In Switzerland there are no natural geysers, because the hot rock lies far too deep there.

teile.einleitung: The Ivory Coast is a country in West Africa on the Atlantic. Officially it is called **Côte d’Ivoire**. It is the largest cocoa producer in the world.
wichtigste: The official capital is **Yamoussoukro**.
The largest city and economic centre is **Abidjan**.
The name comes from the earlier trade in ivory.
The official name is **Côte d’Ivoire** in all languages.
The first president was **Félix Houphouët-Boigny**.
The Ivory Coast has been independent since 1960.
The national football team is called “Les Éléphants”.

abschnitte.text: European traders used to buy a lot of **ivory** on this coast, that is, the tusks of elephants. This is how the coast got its name. In French it is called **Côte d’Ivoire**: côte means coast and ivoire ivory. The country wishes this French name to be used in all languages. The elephant is still the heraldic animal today.

The Ivory Coast was a **colony of France**. In 1960 it became independent, and French is still the official language. The first president was **Félix Houphouët-Boigny**, who led the country until his death in 1993. Later there were political crises and fighting in the country, but since then the situation has calmed again. Besides French, people speak many local languages.

**Yamoussoukro**, the birthplace of Houphouët-Boigny, was declared the capital in 1983. There stands the huge **Basilica of Our Lady of Peace**, consecrated in 1990. It is among the largest churches in the world and recalls St Peter’s Basilica in Rome. **Abidjan** is much bigger. The city lies on a lagoon on the Atlantic, has a large port, and many companies and embassies have their seat there.

The Ivory Coast grows more **cocoa** than any other country. The beans grow on trees on many small farms. Chocolate is made from cocoa, and in Switzerland too, part of the cocoa beans come from here. Besides this, coffee, cashew nuts and rubber, for example, are grown.

In the west lies **Taï National Park**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It protects one of the last large rainforests in West Africa. There **chimpanzees** crack nuts with stones and pieces of wood, so they use tools. Football is very popular: the national team “Les Éléphants” has won the Africa Cup several times, most recently in 2024 at home.

gewusst: The Ivory Coast is one of the few countries that ask that their name not be translated.
The chimpanzees in Taï National Park pass on their nut-cracking technique to the younger animals.

teile.einleitung: A drumlin is an elongated, gently rounded hill shaped by a glacier in the Ice Age. Drumlins often occur in groups and give the landscape a wavy look. A particularly beautiful drumlin landscape lies in the Zurich Oberland.
wichtigste: A drumlin is a streamlined hill made of ground moraine.
Its long axis lies parallel to the former direction of flow of the glacier.
The stoss side, facing the glacier, is steeper.
Its shape is often compared to an upturned spoon.
Many drumlins together form a drumlin swarm.
The word drumlin comes from Irish.

abschnitte.text: During the **Ice Ages**, huge glaciers covered large parts of Switzerland and northern Europe. Beneath the ice lay a layer of clay, sand and stones, the **ground moraine**. The flowing ice shaped this material into elongated hills, the **drumlins**. Exactly how this happened is still discussed among experts. What is certain is that the hills show the direction in which the ice flowed.

A drumlin often looks like an **upturned spoon**. Its **long axis** lies **parallel to the direction of flow** of the former glacier. The side from which the ice came is called the **stoss side** and is usually steeper. The other side slopes away more gently and over a longer distance. Drumlins are often a few hundred metres long and ten to several dozen metres high.

In the **Zurich Oberland**, roughly between Wetzikon, Hinwil and Bubikon, many drumlins lie side by side. Such a group of similarly aligned hills is called a **drumlin swarm**. The landscape is protected in the **Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments**. Between the hills there are often damp hollows with bogs and small lakes.

abschnitte.titel: The name and examples from Ireland
abschnitte.text: The word **drumlin** comes from **Irish** and means something like little ridge. In Ireland drumlins are very common. In **Clew Bay** on the west coast, over a hundred drumlins were flooded by the sea. Today they rise out of the water as small, green islands. There are also many drumlins in Canada, Scotland and around Lake Constance.

gewusst: From the shape of a drumlin, experts can still tell today in which direction a glacier flowed thousands of years ago.
Clew Bay is said to have so many islands that, according to legend, you could visit a different one for every day of the year.

teile.einleitung: **Tierra del Fuego** (“Land of Fire”) is a group of islands at the southern tip of South America. It belongs partly to Chile and partly to Argentina and lies as far south as hardly any other inhabited land.
wichtigste: Tierra del Fuego lies at the southern tip of South America, separated from the mainland by the Strait of Magellan.
The name comes from the fires of the native people, which sailors saw from their ships.
The main island is divided between Chile and Argentina.
The border there runs along a line of longitude.
The Canadian beaver, introduced from North America in 1946, now badly damages the forests.

abschnitte.text: When the fleet of **Ferdinand Magellan** sailed through the strait in the south of South America in 1520, the sailors saw many **fires** on land. These fires came from the **native people**, who warmed themselves with them. The area therefore got the name “Land of Fire”. The native people, for example the Selk’nam and the Yamana, lived from hunting and fishing. Today only a few of their descendants still live there.

The main island, the **Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego**, is divided between **Chile** and **Argentina**. The border there runs as a straight line along a **line of longitude**. The full name of the Argentine province is “Tierra del Fuego, Antarctica and South Atlantic Islands”. It therefore also lays claim to areas in **Antarctica** and islands in the **South Atlantic**. These claims are disputed internationally.

In 1946 **Canadian beavers** were brought from North America to Tierra del Fuego, because people wanted to earn money from their fur. But in Tierra del Fuego the beavers have hardly any natural enemies. They multiplied strongly and build dams everywhere. In doing so they fell trees and flood large areas of forest. The trees there hardly grow back after being felled. The beavers are therefore regarded today as a big problem for the forests.

abschnitte.titel: Life at the end of the world
abschnitte.text: The climate in Tierra del Fuego is cool, windy and often rainy. There are mountains, glaciers, forests and wide grasslands with many sheep. The Argentine city of **Ushuaia** on the **Beagle Channel** is regarded as one of the southernmost cities in the world. Many ships set off from there for Antarctica. South of the main island, on a small island, lies the famous **Cape Horn**.

gewusst: The Beagle Channel is named after the ship on which Charles Darwin also visited this region.
In Ushuaia a small railway runs that used to take prisoners to cut wood and is often called the “Train at the End of the World”.

teile.einleitung: The Gini coefficient is a number used to measure how equally or unequally income or wealth is spread in a country. It lies between 0 and 1.
wichtigste: The Gini coefficient was introduced by the Italian statistician Corrado Gini in 1912.
A value of 0 means complete equality, and a value of 1 means maximum inequality.
On a graph it is based on the Lorenz curve.
Taxes and social transfers typically lower the Gini coefficient.
In Switzerland, wealth is spread much more unequally than income.
The Gini does not show how high the level of income is.

abschnitte.text: The **Gini coefficient** was introduced in 1912 by the Italian statistician **Corrado Gini**. It sums up how income or wealth is distributed in a single number. At **0**, everyone would have exactly the same amount. At **1**, one single person would have everything and everybody else nothing. The higher the value, the more unequal the distribution. It is often multiplied by 100 and given as a number between 0 and 100.

On a graph, the Gini is based on the **Lorenz curve**. You put all people in order from the poorest to the richest and plot which share of the population has which share of the income. With complete equality this would be a straight line, the **line of equality**. The more unequal the distribution, the more the curve sags. The Gini is the area between the line and the curve divided by the whole area under the line. If the area in between is 0.15 and the area under the line is 0.5, the Gini is 0.15 divided by 0.5, which is **0.3**.

The **World Bank** and other organisations calculate the Gini for many countries. **South Africa** has had one of the highest income Gini values in the world for years. Scandinavian countries tend to have low values. What matters is whether the Gini is calculated before or after **taxes and social transfers**. Through taxes, pensions such as the AVS (old-age insurance) and other support, the value typically **falls**.

You can calculate the Gini for **income** and for **wealth**. In Switzerland, wealth is spread **much more unequally** than income. One reason is that wealth often grows over a long time and is inherited. Many people have only a little savings, while a few have a great deal. The Federal Statistical Office regularly publishes figures on this.

The Gini only shows how unequally things are shared out, not how **high the level of income** is. A poor country and a rich country can have the same value. It also does not reveal whether the inequality is more at the top or at the bottom. That is why there are additional measures. The **Palma ratio** compares the income share of the richest 10 per cent with that of the poorest 40 per cent. The **S80/S20 ratio** compares the income of the richest 20 per cent with that of the poorest 20 per cent.

gewusst: The Lorenz curve is named after the American economist Max Lorenz, who described it in 1905.
A Gini of exactly 0 or exactly 1 does not occur in any country in reality.

teile.einleitung: In an **oil refinery**, raw crude oil is separated into many useful products. Only there do petrol, diesel, heating oil and other substances come out of the dark crude oil.
wichtigste: A refinery processes crude oil into products such as petrol, diesel and heating oil.
The most important step is **distillation**: the oil is heated and separated into its components.
The only refinery in Switzerland still operating is in Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel (as of 2025).
The refinery in Collombey in the Valais was shut down in 2015.
A large part of the fuel comes into Switzerland already processed from abroad.

abschnitte.text: Crude oil is a mixture of many different substances. In the refinery it is first heated strongly and led into a tall tower. There the vapours rise and cool. Light substances such as gas and petrol collect at the top, and heavy ones such as heating oil and bitumen at the bottom. This process is called **distillation**. After that the products are cleaned further and improved.

From a refinery come **petrol** and **diesel** for cars, **kerosene** for aeroplanes and **heating oil** for houses. From the heavy residues comes **bitumen**, which is needed for road surfaces. Other components go to the chemical industry, which makes plastics from them, for example. Hardly any of the crude oil is left unused.

In the past there were two refineries in Switzerland. The one at **Collombey** in the Valais was shut down in 2015. Since then the refinery at **Cressier** in the canton of Neuchâtel has been the only one still in operation (as of 2025). It receives its crude oil through a **pipeline** from the Mediterranean coast in France. A large part of the fuel, however, is imported into Switzerland already processed, by ship on the Rhine, by rail or by road.

gewusst: A refinery works day and night without a break, because starting up the large plants takes a long time.
To ensure supply in crises, Switzerland has to hold compulsory stocks of fuel and heating oil.

teile.einleitung: The Galápagos Islands lie in the Pacific and belong to Ecuador. They are famous for their special animals, which often exist nowhere else in the world.
wichtigste: The Galápagos Islands were formed from volcanoes.
The Equator runs right through the island group.
Famous are the giant tortoises and the marine iguanas.
Charles Darwin visited the islands in 1835.
Since 1978 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The main town of the province is Puerto Baquerizo Moreno.

abschnitte.text: The **Galápagos Islands** lie in the **Pacific**, about 1,000 kilometres off the coast of **Ecuador**. They are the tops of **volcanoes** that rise out of the sea. Some volcanoes still erupt today. The **Equator** runs right through the island group. It divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half.

Famous are the **giant tortoises**. They grow to weigh over 200 kilograms and can live to a very great age. The name of the islands comes from the Spanish word “galápago” for tortoise. The **marine iguana** is the only lizard that swims and dives in the sea. It eats **algae** from the rocks under water.

On the islands lives the **Galápagos penguin**, even though the sun shines hot. Cool sea water from the south brings it enough fish. It is the only penguin that lives so close to the Equator. **Sea lions**, cormorants and many seabirds also live here.

The researcher **Charles Darwin** visited the islands in **1835** on the ship Beagle. He noticed that the **finches** have differently shaped **beaks** depending on the island. The beaks suit the food in each case. These observations later helped him with his theory of the **evolution of species**. That is why these birds are called Darwin’s finches today.

In 1535 the Bishop of Panama, **Tomás de Berlanga**, discovered the islands by chance. His ship had drifted off course in a calm. At that time the islands were uninhabited. Today some tens of thousands of people live there. The main town of the province is **Puerto Baquerizo Moreno** on San Cristóbal, and the largest settlement is Puerto Ayora. In **1978** the islands were one of the first twelve sites to be put on the **UNESCO World Heritage** list.

gewusst: Many animals on the Galápagos have hardly any fear of people, because for a long time they knew no enemies on land.
To protect nature, visitors may enter many places only with trained guides.

teile.einleitung: The one-child policy was a rule of the Chinese government under which most families were allowed only one child. It applied from 1979/1980 to 2015 and was meant to slow the strong growth of the population. Its consequences shape China to this day.
wichtigste: The one-child policy applied in China from 1979/1980 to 2015.
From 2016 it was replaced by the two-child policy.
Since 2021 China has officially allowed three children per couple.
It was enforced mainly with fines and disadvantages at work.
Exceptions applied to ethnic minorities and many farming families.
One consequence is a clear surplus of men.
According to official figures, China’s population has been shrinking since 2022.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 1970s, almost a billion people already lived in China. The government feared that the country would not have enough food, housing and work for everyone. It therefore introduced the **one-child policy** in **1979/1980**. Most married couples in the cities were now allowed only one child. In this way the government wanted to slow **population growth** and develop the economy faster.

Anyone who did not keep to the rule had to expect **fines**. **Disadvantages at work** also often threatened, such as losing a job with the state. The rule did not apply equally to everyone, however. For **ethnic minorities** and many **farming families** in the countryside there were exceptions or relaxations. Human rights organisations criticised the fact that the state interfered very strongly in the lives of families.

Many children in China grew up without siblings. This gives rise to the so-called **“4-2-1 problem”**: a single child later has to support its **two parents** and **four grandparents**. That is a heavy burden, because China does not have such a dense network of old-age provision as Switzerland has, for example, with the AHV. At the same time, the population is ageing fast.

Another consequence shows in the **sex ratio**. In many families people traditionally wished for a son, who would later look after the parents. Because only one child was allowed, clearly more boys than girls were brought up. Today China has a **clear surplus of men**. Many young men therefore cannot find a partner.

In **2016** the **two-child policy** replaced the old rule. Since **2021**, **three children** per couple have officially been allowed. Even so, few children are born in China today, because housing and education are expensive. Since **2022** the population has been **shrinking**, according to official figures. The **rapid ageing** of society is a big challenge. In 2023, according to UN estimates, China was overtaken by India as the most populous country.

gewusst: The one-child policy applied for about 35 years. In that time a whole generation of only children grew up in China.
Today the Chinese government is trying to encourage families to have more children with money and cheaper housing.

teile.einleitung: Denali in Alaska is the highest mountain in North America. It towers hugely above the flat land around it. Its name comes from the language of the native people.
wichtigste: Denali lies in the US state of Alaska.
According to the 2015 measurement, it is 6,190 metres high.
“Denali” means “the high one” in the language of the Koyukon Athabaskans.
On land, it has the greatest height difference from base to summit.
It was first climbed in 1913.
Because it is high and far to the north, it is extremely cold there.

abschnitte.titel: The highest mountain in North America
abschnitte.text: **Denali** stands in the Alaska Range in **Alaska**. A measurement in **2015** gave a height of **6,190 metres**. That makes it almost 1,400 metres higher than Mont Blanc. It is one of the **Seven Summits**, the highest mountains on the seven continents, which many mountaineers want to climb.

Denali rises from a plain that lies only a few hundred metres above sea level. From base to summit it measures about 5,500 metres. That is the **greatest height difference** of any mountain on land. Mount Everest is higher, but it stands on the high Tibetan Plateau, so its visible height difference is smaller.

In the language of the **Koyukon Athabaskans**, a people native to Alaska, **“Denali”** means “**the high one**”. From 1917 the mountain was officially called Mount McKinley, after a US president. In 2015 it officially got the name Denali back. In 2025 the US government ordered the name Mount McKinley again, but in Alaska and in the national park people still say Denali.

It is **especially cold** on Denali because it is **high** and lies **far to the north**, not far from the Arctic Circle. There are violent storms and temperatures far below minus 30 degrees. In **1913** a group of four men reached the summit for the first time. Today many mountaineers attempt the climb every year, which usually takes two to three weeks.

gewusst: From base to summit, Denali is taller on land than any other mountain, even Mount Everest.
On clear days Denali can be seen from the city of Anchorage, although it is over 200 kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: Spices are parts of plants that give food flavour, aroma and sometimes colour. Many come from warm countries and were once as valuable as gold.
wichtigste: Spices come from different parts of plants: bark, roots, seeds, flowers or fruits.
Cinnamon is made from the bark of a tree.
Pepper used to be so expensive that it was called “black gold”.
Turmeric colours curry powder yellow.
The Moluccas in Asia used to be called the Spice Islands.
Saffron is grown in the Valais village of Mund.

abschnitte.text: Spices come from quite different parts of a plant. **Cinnamon** is the dried **bark** of a tree, which rolls up into sticks as it dries. **Ginger** is a hot rhizome, a kind of tuber that grows in the ground. **Cloves** are dried flower buds and look like small **nails**. Peppercorns are the small fruits of a **climbing plant**.

**Pepper** originally comes from India. In the Middle Ages it had to be brought to Europe over long routes and was therefore very expensive. It was called **“black gold”**, and sometimes people even paid with peppercorns. Black, green and white pepper, by the way, come from the same plant. They are only harvested and processed differently.

Some spices give food not only flavour but also colour. **Turmeric** is a bright yellow root and colours **curry powder** yellow. Curry, by the way, is not a single spice but a mixture of many. **Cinnamon** goes well with sweet dishes: in Switzerland people like to sprinkle it with sugar on **rice pudding**. Gingerbread and cinnamon stars also contain a lot of cinnamon.

The **Moluccas** are a group of islands in present-day Indonesia. In the past, cloves and nutmeg grew only there, so they were called the **Spice Islands**. To get hold of the valuable spices, European sailors looked for a sea route to Asia. Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498 by sea round Africa. Later European powers fought hard over the spice trade.

**Saffron** is one of the most expensive spices in the world. It consists of the fine, red threads in the flower of a kind of crocus. Every flower has to be picked by hand, and for one gram you need a great many flowers. In the Valais village of **Mund**, saffron has been grown for centuries. It colours dishes such as risotto a beautiful yellow.

gewusst: The saffron from Mund has a protected designation of origin (AOP).
For a single gram of saffron you need the threads of over a hundred flowers.

teile.einleitung: In **fair trade**, women and men farmers in poorer countries are meant to get a fair price for their products. In Switzerland such goods are often recognised by the label **Max Havelaar**.
wichtigste: The Fairtrade label is called **Max Havelaar** in Switzerland.
The name comes from a character in a novel by the Dutch author Multatuli.
The seal of quality was introduced in the Netherlands in 1988.
Fairtrade guarantees a **minimum price** and a **premium**.
From 1973 the **Banana Women** of Frauenfeld campaigned for fairly traded bananas.
World Fair Trade Day is on the second Saturday in May.

abschnitte.text: Many farmers in Africa, Asia and Latin America get only little money for coffee, cocoa or bananas. **Fair trade** wants to change this. It guarantees producer organisations a **minimum price**, even if the world market price falls. In addition there is a **premium**, with which communities pay for schools, wells or better growing methods, for example. Rules against child labour and for environmental protection are also part of it.

The first seal of quality for fair trade was introduced in 1988 in the **Netherlands**. It was named **Max Havelaar**, after the main character of a novel by **Multatuli** from 1860. In the novel, Max Havelaar stands up against the exploitation of farmers in the then Dutch colony on Java. In Switzerland the Fairtrade label is still known under this name today. Internationally, the umbrella organisation **Fairtrade International** awards the seal.

As early as 1973 the **Banana Women** of **Frauenfeld** campaigned for fair prices. They wanted to know why bananas are so cheap here and the farmers earn so little. With campaigns they drew attention to the problem. In 1997, **bananas** became the first fresh product in Switzerland to go on sale with the Max Havelaar seal. Today fairly traded bananas are available in almost every supermarket.

**World shops** sell only fairly traded goods, whereas supermarkets offer fair products alongside ordinary ones. On the second Saturday in May, **World Fair Trade Day** is celebrated. Critics say that fair trade reaches only a small share of farmers worldwide. Others ask how much of the higher price really reaches the producers. Supporters point out that it gives many families a more secure income.

gewusst: Switzerland is among the countries where the most money per head is spent on Fairtrade products.
Besides food, there are also fairly traded flowers, cotton and sports balls.

teile.einleitung: Longitude tells you how far east or west of the prime meridian a place lies. The lines for it are called meridians and run from the North Pole to the South Pole.
wichtigste: Meridians run from the North Pole to the South Pole and meet at the two poles.
Counting starts at the prime meridian through Greenwich near London and goes up to 180° east and 180° west.
With one degree between each, there are about 360 meridians around the Earth.
The distance between two meridians gets smaller towards the poles, down to zero.
Switzerland lies roughly between 6° and 10.5° east.
In the 18th century John Harrison built an accurate marine clock for determining longitude.

abschnitte.text: The **meridians** are imaginary half circles that run from the **North Pole** to the **South Pole**. At the two poles all the meridians meet. Counting starts at the **prime meridian**, which passes through the observatory at **Greenwich** near London. This was agreed at an international conference in 1884. From there you count up to 180° to the east and up to 180° to the west.

With one degree between each, there are about **360 meridians** around the Earth. At the Equator, two neighbouring meridians lie a good 111 kilometres apart. Towards the poles they move ever closer together, until at the poles the distance is **zero**. Switzerland lies roughly between **6° and 10.5° east**. Geneva lies furthest to the west, and the Münstertal valley in Graubünden furthest to the east.

The Earth turns once on its axis in 24 hours, that is, through 360°. This means that **15 degrees** of longitude correspond to one hour. That is why the **time zones** are closely linked to longitude. If you compare the time at your place with the time at the prime meridian, you can work out your longitude. Opposite the prime meridian, at about 180°, runs the **Date Line**.

At sea it was for a long time very difficult to determine longitude. For this you needed a clock that keeps accurate time even on a rocking ship. The English clockmaker **John Harrison** built such accurate marine clocks, so-called **chronometers**, in the 18th century. With them sailors could work out their position much more reliably. Today satellite navigation does this.

The **metre** too has to do with the meridians. In France in the 1790s it was defined as **one ten-millionth** of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator, measured along a meridian. For this, researchers surveyed a stretch between Dunkirk and Barcelona. Today the metre is defined more precisely through the speed of light.

gewusst: Because the metre was defined in this way, the circumference of the Earth over the poles is roughly 40,000 kilometres.
At the North Pole you can walk round all the meridians in a few steps.

teile.einleitung: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation, **ENSO** for short, is a natural swing of sea and air in the tropical Pacific. It has three states: El Niño, La Niña and neutral years in between.
wichtigste: ENSO links the sea temperature with the air pressure over the Pacific.
**El Niño** is the warm phase and **La Niña** the cold phase.
El Niño occurs irregularly about every 2 to 7 years.
The **Southern Oscillation Index** compares the air pressure of Tahiti and Darwin.
In El Niño, the **Walker circulation** weakens.
Measurements are often made in the **Niño 3.4** region.
Strong El Niño years temporarily raise the global temperature.

abschnitte.text: The second part of the name, **Southern Oscillation**, describes a seesaw in air pressure. If the pressure over the eastern Pacific is high, it is low over Indonesia and Australia, and the other way round. The **SOI** is traditionally calculated from the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin in Australia. A clearly negative value points to El Niño, and a positive one to La Niña.

In normal years, moist air rises over the warm water near Indonesia. At height it flows east and sinks again over the cool eastern Pacific. At the surface the **trade winds** blow back to the west. This cycle is called the **Walker circulation**. In El Niño, the rising shifts to the east, and the cycle becomes weaker.

In El Niño, a thick layer of warm water settles off South America. It prevents nutrient-rich deep water from rising. The plankton declines, and the anchovy shoals off Peru fall in number. On the coasts of Peru and Ecuador there is **heavy rain** and flooding, while Indonesia and Australia often suffer from drought.

La Niña is the counterpart. The trade winds are stronger and drive even more warm water to the west. Off South America, especially a lot of cold deep water rises, and the eastern Pacific becomes unusually cool. Then it often rains more than usual in South-East Asia and Australia.

Experts observe the water temperature in certain areas of the sea. Especially important is the **Niño 3.4** region in the central equatorial Pacific. The US weather agency NOAA speaks of El Niño when the water there is permanently at least 0.5 °C warmer than average, and of La Niña when it is at least 0.5 °C cooler. Measuring buoys and satellites supply the data.

gewusst: The years 1998 and 2016 followed strong El Niños and each was among the warmest years ever measured at the time.
The Walker circulation is named after the British researcher Gilbert Walker, who studied the air pressure seesaw about a hundred years ago.

teile.einleitung: An early warning system detects dangers early and warns people before something happens. This leaves time to get to safety, for example in storms, floods or tsunamis.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the sirens are tested every year on the first Wednesday in February.
At the general alarm you should listen to the radio and follow the instructions of the authorities.
The water alarm warns when a dam threatens to burst.
The Alertswiss app spreads warnings from the authorities.
The federal natural hazard warnings have 5 danger levels.
Earthquake early warning systems give only seconds of advance notice.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are about 5,000 sirens. Every year on the **first Wednesday in February** they are checked to see whether they work. The **general alarm** is a rising and falling wail. Then you should **listen to the radio** and follow the instructions of the authorities. The **water alarm** consists of low continuous tones. It warns people below large dams when a **dam threatens to burst**. Then you must leave the area at once.

The federal **Alertswiss** app spreads alarms, warnings and information from the authorities. It complements the sirens and the radio. For natural hazards such as storms, floods or avalanches there are warnings in **five danger levels**. Level 1 means no or slight danger, and level 5 very great danger.

A **tsunami** is a huge wave that is usually caused by an undersea earthquake. Sensors on the sea floor measure the **water pressure**. If a tsunami wave passes over them, the pressure rises slightly. The data go via **buoys and satellites** to warning centres. After the devastating tsunami in the Indian Ocean in 2004, such systems were greatly expanded.

Earthquakes **cannot be predicted**. But an early warning system detects the fast first waves of an earthquake. It warns before the destructive waves arrive. This gives only **seconds** of advance notice, enough for example to brake trains. At volcanoes, experts measure **small earthquakes, ground uplift and gases**. When magma rises, these values often change.

gewusst: At the annual siren test, the public does not have to do anything.
For avalanches, the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos issues an avalanche bulletin.

teile.einleitung: The Three Gorges Dam in China holds back the Yangtze, the longest river in Asia. Its power station is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world. The structure supplies a lot of electricity and protects against floods, but it also has major consequences for people and nature.
wichtigste: The Three Gorges Dam stands in China on the Yangtze.
It lies near the city of Yichang.
Its power station is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world.
Since 2012 the power station has been fully in operation.
The reservoir is about 600 kilometres long.
More than a million people had to be resettled.
Besides electricity, protection against floods is an important purpose.

abschnitte.text: The dam stands on the **Yangtze** in Hubei Province, near the city of **Yichang**. It takes its name from three famous, narrow gorges upstream. Building began in 1994. The dam wall is over two kilometres long. Behind it a huge **reservoir** formed, stretching about **600 kilometres** upstream. That is clearly longer than the whole of Switzerland from west to east.

In the power station, dozens of huge **turbines** turn. Together they produce more electricity than any other hydroelectric power station in the world. Since **2012** the plant has been **fully in operation**. The electricity supplies millions of homes and factories in China. Because hydropower gives off no carbon dioxide, China has to burn less coal as a result.

In the past, the Yangtze burst its banks again and again and caused severe damage. An important purpose of the dam is therefore **flood protection**. Before the rainy season, the reservoir is lowered so that it can take in large amounts of water. In this way the cities and fields downstream are meant to be better protected. The dam cannot prevent floods completely, however.

The Yangtze is an important waterway for cargo ships. So that they can get past the dam, there are large **locks** with several stages. For smaller ships a **ship lift** was also built. It raises or lowers ships in a trough filled with water, as in a lift. This is much quicker than going through the locks.

The reservoir flooded towns, villages, fields and ancient cultural sites. **More than a million people** therefore had to move. Critics also point to consequences for nature: the river changes, and the reservoir holds back mud. Supporters stress the clean electricity and the flood protection. The project is still argued over today.

gewusst: The ship lift at the Three Gorges Dam is among the largest in the world.
The three gorges after which the dam is named are called Qutang, Wu and Xiling.

teile.einleitung: Elephants are the largest land animals on Earth. They live wild in Africa and Asia and are instantly recognisable by their long trunk and big ears.
wichtigste: Wild elephants live in **Africa and Asia**.
The long nose is called the **trunk**.
The long teeth are called **tusks** and are made of ivory.
African elephants have bigger ears than Asian ones.
Elephants are **plant eaters**.
An older female elephant leads the herd.
A young elephant is called a **calf**.

abschnitte.text: There are **African elephants** and **Asian elephants**. In Africa a distinction is also made between the savanna elephant and the smaller forest elephant. African elephants are usually bigger and have very large ears. Asian elephants have smaller ears and a rather rounded back. There are no wild elephants on other continents.

The **trunk** is the nose and upper lip together. It has very many muscles and is therefore strong and flexible. With it an elephant can smell, drink, grasp food and shower itself with water or dust. The **tusks** are very long incisor teeth made of **ivory**. With them elephants dig for water or peel bark from trees.

Elephants eat only plants: grass, leaves, twigs, bark and fruit. Because they are so big, they eat a great deal every day and spend a large part of the day eating. In the ears there are many **blood vessels**. When an elephant flaps its ears, the blood cools down, and it feels less hot.

Female elephants and their calves live together in a **herd**. An experienced older female leads it and knows the ways to water and food. At about 22 months, that is, almost two years, the pregnancy is the longest of all land animals. A **calf** stays with its mother for many years and learns from the whole herd. The bulls mostly live alone or in groups of their own.

Elephants are endangered because their habitat is getting smaller and because poachers hunt them for ivory. The worldwide trade in ivory has therefore been banned in principle since 1989. In Zurich Zoo, Asian elephants live in the large **Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park**, where they have plenty of room to walk and bathe.

gewusst: An elephant’s trunk has many thousands of muscles, more than a human’s whole body.
Elephants can communicate through deep rumbling sounds that carry for several kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conqueror, also called a conquistador. With a small force he conquered the empire of the Incas in South America in the 16th century and founded the city of Lima.
wichtigste: Pizarro came from Trujillo in Spain.
In 1532 he took the Inca ruler Atahualpa prisoner.
Afterwards the Spaniards conquered the Inca Empire.
In 1535 Pizarro founded the city of Lima, today the capital of Peru.
In 1541 he was killed in Lima by his opponents.

abschnitte.text: Pizarro was born around 1476 in **Trujillo** in the Spanish region of Extremadura. As a young man he went to the Spanish territories in America. He heard of a rich land in the south with a great deal of **gold**. After several voyages of exploration he received permission from the Spanish king to conquer this land.

The **Inca Empire** was at that time the largest empire in America. But it had been weakened by a war between two brothers over the throne. In addition, many people had died of diseases that the Europeans had brought in. In 1532 Pizarro took the Inca ruler **Atahualpa** prisoner at **Cajamarca**. Although Atahualpa had a huge treasure brought as a ransom, he was executed in 1533.

After the death of Atahualpa, the Spaniards conquered the capital **Cusco** and large parts of the empire. Pizarro, however, wanted a capital close to the sea. He therefore founded the city of **Lima** in **1535**. It became the centre of Spanish rule in South America. Today Lima is the capital of **Peru**.

Among the conquerors a quarrel soon broke out over power and wealth, especially with his former partner **Diego de Almagro**. In 1541 Pizarro was killed in Lima by followers of Almagro. For the Incas the conquest meant the end of their empire. Today Pizarro’s role is viewed very critically.

gewusst: Pizarro was distantly related to the conqueror of the Aztec Empire, Hernán Cortés.
Pizarro began the conquest with only a few hundred men.

teile.einleitung: The date palm is one of the oldest crop plants in the world. It grows in hot, dry regions, especially in oases. Its sweet fruits, the dates, have been eaten for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Date palms grow in the desert mainly in oases.
They need plenty of sun and moist soil.
A date palm can grow to about 20 metres tall.
Its large leaves are called fronds.
Only the female palms bear fruit.
Dates taste very sweet.
In Switzerland, dates are mostly bought dried.

abschnitte.text: The date palm grows in North Africa and the Middle East. In the desert it is found mainly in **oases**, where groundwater lies close to the surface. It needs **a lot of sun** and **moist soil**. An old saying says that the date palm wants its feet in water and its head in fire. In its shade, other plants such as vegetables can thrive.

A date palm can grow to **about 20 metres** tall. Its trunk is slender and carries a crown of large, feathery leaves at the top. These leaves are called **fronds**. They can be several metres long. People weave baskets, mats and roofs from the fronds.

Date palms have **male** and **female** trees. Only the **female** ones bear fruit. For dates to form, the pollen from the male flowers has to reach the female flowers. On plantations, people often pollinate the flowers by hand. In this way a palm can bear many kilos of dates every year.

Dates taste **very sweet** because they contain a lot of sugar. They grow in large bunches. In Switzerland they are mostly bought **dried**, because they keep for a long time that way. Many **Muslims** traditionally break their fast in the evening during the fasting month of **Ramadan** with a date and a little water.

abschnitte.titel: A sign on a coat of arms
abschnitte.text: The date palm is an important symbol in many countries. On the **coat of arms of Saudi Arabia** stands a **palm tree** above two crossed swords. The palm stands there for growth and life. The date palm was already being grown in Mesopotamia thousands of years ago.

gewusst: A date palm can live to over 100 years old.
On plantations, workers climb the palms to pollinate the flowers by hand.

teile.einleitung: The **fertility rate** is an important figure in population studies. It shows how many children a woman has on average over her lifetime, and it helps predict whether a population will grow or shrink.
wichtigste: The total fertility rate gives the average number of children per woman.
In industrialised countries, about 2.1 children per woman are needed for a population to maintain itself without immigration.
Worldwide, the fertility rate was about 2.2 children per woman around 2024, according to the UN.
Africa is the continent with the highest fertility rates.
Around 2023 South Korea had the lowest fertility rate in the world, under 0.8.
The **crude birth rate** relates births to 1,000 inhabitants.

abschnitte.text: The **total fertility rate** shows how many children a woman would have on average if today’s conditions stayed the same. If it is about **2.1** in an industrialised country, the population stays roughly the same size without immigration. This is called the **replacement level**. It is slightly above 2 because not all children survive to adulthood. If the rate is below it, the population shrinks in the long term, provided nobody immigrates.

Another figure is the **crude birth rate**. It counts the births in a year per 1,000 inhabitants. An example: a country has 4 million inhabitants and 60,000 births. You calculate 60,000 divided by 4,000, which gives **15 per 1,000**. This figure depends strongly on how old the population is. That is why experts prefer to compare countries using the fertility rate.

Worldwide, the fertility rate was about **2.2 children per woman** around 2024, according to the UN. In the past it was much higher. It is highest today in **Africa**, where in some countries families with many children are usual. The lowest around 2023 was in **South Korea**, with under 0.8 children per woman. Many countries in Europe and East Asia are also clearly below 2.1.

Experience shows that **better education** for girls and women lowers the fertility rate most strongly. Those who stay longer at school and learn a profession often start a family later. Good health care also plays a part: when fewer children die early, families often want fewer children. In Switzerland, women are on average about **31 years** old at the birth of their first child (as of 2023). The fertility rate there was about 1.3 in 2023.

gewusst: A low fertility rate leads to a rising share of older people, which sets the AHV, for example, new tasks.
In Switzerland the population is growing despite a low fertility rate, mainly because of immigration.

teile.einleitung: The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta is the largest river delta on Earth. Here two mighty rivers run together into the Bay of Bengal.
wichtigste: At over 100,000 square kilometres, the delta is the largest in the world.
It lies in Bangladesh and in the Indian state of West Bengal.
In Bangladesh the Ganges is called the Padma and the Brahmaputra the Jamuna.
On the coast lie the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove area on Earth.
The Bhola cyclone of 1970 is among the deadliest cyclones in history.
Many wells are contaminated with natural arsenic.

abschnitte.text: The **Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta** covers over **100,000 square kilometres**. That is more than twice the area of Switzerland. It is often also called the **Bengal Delta**. The largest part lies in **Bangladesh**, and the western part in the Indian state of **West Bengal**. The land is very flat and fertile, and a great many people live here.

After entering Bangladesh, the main arm of the Ganges is called the **Padma**. The main course of the Brahmaputra is called the **Jamuna** there. It must not be confused with the Indian Yamuna, a tributary of the Ganges. In India the **Hooghly** also branches off as a distributary. The rivers bring huge amounts of mud from the Himalayas.

On the coast lie the **Sundarbans**, the largest **mangrove forest area** on Earth. They are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. The mangroves protect the hinterland from **storm surges**. One of the best-known populations of the **Bengal tiger** lives here. The tigers are adapted to salt water and to swimming.

Because the land is so flat, **cyclones** and storm surges are especially dangerous. In November 1970 the **Bhola cyclone** hit the coast of what was then East Pakistan, today Bangladesh. An estimated 300,000 to 500,000 people lost their lives. It is regarded as one of the deadliest cyclones in history. Today there are warning systems and protective structures.

The sediments of the delta naturally contain **arsenic**, a poisonous substance. It dissolves in the **groundwater**. Many people get their drinking water from wells. As a result, millions of people drink contaminated water. People are trying to build safe wells and to test the water.

gewusst: In the delta the rivers keep changing their course, so that islands appear and disappear.
The tides of the sea reach far into the delta.

teile.einleitung: The hippopotamus, also called the river horse, is one of the largest land animals on Earth. It lives in Africa and spends the day mostly in the water.
wichtigste: The hippopotamus lives in rivers and lakes in Africa.
By day it lies in the water, and at night it eats grass on land.
Its eyes, ears and nose sit on top of its head.
A reddish fluid protects its skin from the sun.
It is very dangerous and defends its territory fiercely.
Its closest relatives are whales, not horses.

abschnitte.text: Hippopotamuses live in **rivers and lakes** south of the Sahara. They spend the hot day mostly in the water. This keeps their sensitive skin moist and cool. **Eyes, ears and nostrils** sit on top of the head. The animal can therefore almost completely submerge and still breathe and see. It can hardly swim properly: it **walks or bounds along the bottom**.

Hippopotamuses are **plant eaters** and eat mainly **grass**. To do so they leave the water **at night**. They often walk for kilometres. Because they are so big, they need a great deal of food every night. In the morning they return to the water.

The skin of a hippopotamus dries out quickly in the sun. The animal therefore makes a **reddish fluid** on its skin. It acts like a **sunscreen** and keeps the skin supple. In the past people believed that the hippopotamus sweated blood. That is not true, however.

Hippopotamuses look easy-going but are **very dangerous**. They defend their territory fiercely and can attack with surprising speed. They are among the most dangerous animals in Africa. When a hippopotamus opens its mouth wide, it shows its long **canine teeth**. This is a threat to other animals.

Although it is called a “horse”, the hippopotamus is not related to the horse. Researchers have found that its closest living relatives are the **whales**. Besides the big hippopotamus there is also the much smaller **pygmy hippopotamus**. It lives in the forests of West Africa.

gewusst: A hippopotamus can stay under water for several minutes without surfacing.
The name “hippopotamus” comes from Greek and means river horse.

teile.einleitung: Desertification means that fertile land in dry regions turns into land like a desert. Plants disappear, and the soil loses its strength. The causes are long droughts, but above all people too.
wichtigste: Desertification means the spreading of desert conditions.
Long droughts make it especially severe.
Overgrazing by too many animals is an important human cause.
The Sahel zone south of the Sahara is particularly threatened.
Wrong irrigation can make the soil salty.
In 1994 the UN adopted the UNCCD convention.
The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is on 17 June.

abschnitte.text: In **desertification**, land in dry regions gradually becomes infertile. It is not simply a matter of existing deserts such as the Sahara spreading. Rather, the soil is destroyed in many places by climate and use. Without plants, the wind carries the fertile soil away, and rain washes it off.

**Long droughts** make desertification especially severe. Then there are people: if too many animals graze on too small an area, they eat the plants right down to the roots. This is called **overgrazing**. Cutting down trees for firewood also does harm. If dry soils are **irrigated** in the wrong way, the water evaporates and leaves salt behind. The soil becomes **salty**, and hardly anything grows any more.

The **Sahel zone**, a belt south of the Sahara, is particularly threatened. Many people there live from farming and herding. In the Sahel, it is above all **overgrazing by too many animals** that contributes to desertification. When the land no longer yields anything, some families have to move away.

The **“Great Green Wall”** is a project of African countries. Right across Africa, from Senegal to Djibouti, **trees** and other plants are to grow. They are meant to hold the soil in place and make the land fertile again. The project was started in 2007 and is making only slow progress.

In **1994** the UN adopted the **Convention to Combat Desertification**, abbreviated **UNCCD**. Almost all countries in the world have signed it. Every year on **17 June** is the World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought. What can help is **planting trees**, **sparing pastures**, using water carefully and building stone walls that hold back rainwater.

gewusst: The roots of plants such as bushes also hold the soil in place like a net.
Farmers in the Sahel have learned to let tree stumps on their fields sprout again, and in this way new green areas have appeared.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is full of records: the highest mountain, the deepest lake, the largest island or the highest waterfall. Geographical records show how varied and extreme our planet is. Many of these superlatives lie far away, but some are in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth by area.
Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest lake on Earth.
Greenland is the largest island on Earth.
The lowest point on land is at the Dead Sea.
The highest waterfall on Earth, Angel Falls, lies in Venezuela.
At 8,849 metres, Mount Everest is the highest mountain.
The lowest point of the oceans lies in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific.

abschnitte.text: At 8,849 metres, **Mount Everest** in the Himalayas is the highest mountain on Earth. The deepest known point of the oceans is the **Challenger Deep** in the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific, almost 11,000 metres below sea level. If you stood Everest there, its summit would still be over 2,000 metres under water. The lowest point on land lies on the shore of the **Dead Sea** between Israel and Jordan, over 400 metres below sea level.

The **Caspian Sea** between Europe and Asia is the largest lake on Earth by area, about nine times as big as Switzerland. Although it is called a sea, it is a lake with no connection to the ocean, and its water is slightly salty. **Lake Baikal** in Siberia, at over 1,600 metres, is the deepest lake in the world. It is also the oldest lake on Earth and holds about a fifth of the liquid fresh water of all lakes and rivers.

**Greenland** is the largest island on Earth and belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark, and the largest part of it is covered with ice. Australia counts as a continent and is therefore not counted as an island. The highest waterfall on Earth is **Angel Falls** in Venezuela, where the water plunges almost 1,000 metres. The waterfalls with the greatest volume of water are others, for example the Iguazú Falls in South America.

The **Sahara** in Africa is the largest hot desert on Earth. If you also count cold deserts, Antarctica is the largest desert, because hardly any precipitation falls there. The **Nile** and the **Amazon** dispute the title of the longest river, and depending on the measurement one or the other wins. The Amazon, however, carries by far the most water.

The highest point in Switzerland is the **Dufourspitze** in Valais at 4,634 metres. The lowest point lies on the shore of Lake Maggiore in Ticino, at about 193 metres. The **Great Aletsch Glacier** is the largest glacier in the Alps. The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen are regarded as one of the waterfalls with the most water in Europe.

Some records change over time. Mount Everest was measured anew in 2020, so it is officially 8,849 metres high today. The Dead Sea sinks about a metre every year, because water is taken from it for agriculture and industry. Glaciers too are shrinking because of **global warming**, so their size keeps changing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average height of the sea surface, from which heights are measured.
A very deep, long channel in the sea floor.
The highest degree of comparison, for example biggest, highest, deepest.
Water with very little salt, as in most lakes and rivers.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea the water is so salty that people float on the surface without effort.
Angel Falls is over 40 times as high as the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen.

teile.einleitung: On 26 December 2004 a gigantic undersea earthquake shook the seabed off Sumatra in Indonesia. It set off a **tsunami** that struck coasts all around the Indian Ocean. It was one of the worst natural disasters in recent history.
wichtigste: The quake had a **magnitude of 9.1 to 9.3**.
It is among the three strongest quakes ever recorded.
The Indian Plate pushes under the Eurasian Plate there.
The rupture zone was over **1,000 km** long.
About **230,000 people** lost their lives, most of them in **Indonesia**.
The tsunami even reached **Somalia** in Africa.
After 2004, **early warning systems** were set up in the Indian Ocean.

abschnitte.text: Off the west coast of Sumatra lies the **Sunda Trench**. There the Indo-Australian Plate pushes under the Eurasian Plate by a few centimetres a year. On 26 December 2004 the accumulated tension was released at a stroke. The rupture ran for more than **1,000 km** from northern Sumatra to the Andaman Islands and lasted several minutes. The USGS gives a **magnitude** of 9.1, and some researchers estimated up to 9.3.

The seabed rose with a jerk and pushed huge masses of water. A **tsunami** spread across the whole Indian Ocean. On the coast of **Aceh** in northern Sumatra the waves arrived only about 20 minutes after the quake, and the city of **Banda Aceh** was badly destroyed. About two hours later the waves hit **Sri Lanka**, after a journey of about 1,600 km. Thailand, India and even **Somalia** in Africa were also hit, where the town of Hafun was largely destroyed.

In about a dozen countries, around **230,000 people** lost their lives. It is one of the deadliest tsunamis in history. Most victims were in **Indonesia**, above all in Aceh Province. Among the dead were also many tourists from Europe who were holidaying on the beaches over Christmas, including people from Switzerland. Many countries sent help afterwards.

Before 2004 there was **no tsunami warning system** in the Indian Ocean. With a warning, many people on more distant coasts would have had time to flee. Afterwards several countries set up systems. Germany developed, together with Indonesia, **GITEWS**, the German Indonesian Tsunami Early Warning System. It began operation in 2008.

On the island of **Simeulue**, near the epicentre, only very few people died. After a tsunami in 1907, the residents had passed on a rule that they call **“Smong”**: when the Earth shakes and the sea draws back, flee at once inland. This handed-down warning saved almost everyone’s life.

gewusst: When the sea suddenly draws back far, this can be a sign of an approaching tsunami.
The 2004 quake was so strong that it set the whole Earth vibrating slightly.

teile.einleitung: Japan is one of the countries with the oldest population in the world. Few children are born, and people live for a very long time. As a result, the population is shrinking, and the country has to adapt to many older people.
wichtigste: Japan’s population reached its peak of about 128 million around 2008.
In September 2024, about 29 per cent of people were aged 65 or older.
Japan is regarded as a “super-aged society”.
In 2024 the birth rate was about 1.15 children per woman.
The median age is about 49 years.
Immigration policy has traditionally been very restrictive.
Japan is relying, among other things, on care robots.

abschnitte.text: Around **2008**, about **128 million** people lived in Japan, more than ever before. Since then the number has fallen. One reason is the low **birth rate**: in 2024 there were on average only about **1.15 children** per woman. For a population to stay the same size without immigration, about 2.1 children would be needed.

At the same time, people in Japan live to a very great age, and life expectancy is among the highest in the world. In September 2024, about **29 per cent** of the population were **aged 65 or older**. When the figure is over 21 per cent, this is called a **super-aged society**. The **median age** is about 49 years. This means that half of the people are older than 49.

Many young people move to big cities such as Tokyo. In **rural regions**, mainly older people are left behind. There are many **empty houses** there, which are called “akiya” in Japanese. Schools close, and some villages are in danger of disappearing altogether.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences for the economy and work
abschnitte.text: When there are more older people and fewer young people, the **costs of pensions and health care** rise. At the same time, workers are in short supply. Japan has traditionally had a very **restrictive immigration policy**, so the population hardly grows through immigration. In recent years the country has eased the rules for foreign workers somewhat.

Care in particular is short of people. Japan is therefore developing **care robots** that help with lifting, for example, or keep older people company. Switzerland also knows this issue: the population is getting older, and the financing of the **AHV** is much discussed. In Japan, however, this development is already further advanced.

gewusst: Japan has one of the highest life expectancies in the world.
Japan has one of the highest numbers of people over 100 years old in the world.

teile.einleitung: **Sloths** are the slowest mammals in the world. They live in the rainforests of Central and South America and spend almost their whole lives hanging upside down in the trees.
wichtigste: Sloths live in Central and South America.
They move very slowly and mostly hang in the trees.
With long, curved claws they hold on to the branches.
They eat mainly leaves.
Their fur often looks greenish, because algae grow in it.
About once a week they climb down to the ground to relieve themselves.

abschnitte.text: Sloths live in the tropical forests of **Central and South America**. A distinction is made between **two-toed sloths** and **three-toed sloths**. They move very slowly and sleep many hours a day. With their long, curved **claws** they hang securely from the branches, even in their sleep. On the ground they make slow progress, because their legs are built for hanging.

Sloths eat mainly **leaves**. These contain little energy and are hard to digest. Sloths therefore have a large, multi-part stomach, and digestion takes a very long time. Because they get so little energy, they save wherever they can. Their slowness is therefore a clever way of getting by on little food.

abschnitte.titel: A green coat full of guests
abschnitte.text: In the fur of sloths grow tiny **algae**, which colour it greenish. In this way the animals are well camouflaged among the leaves. Small **moths** and other insects also live in the fur. About once a week the sloth climbs down to the ground to relieve itself. The moths then lay their eggs in the droppings, and the young moths later fly back into the fur of a sloth.

Even though they are slow on land, sloths can **swim** astonishingly well. If a sloth falls from a tree over a river into the water, it paddles to the bank with its long arms. In the water they are even faster than on the ground. Some cross rivers in this way to reach new trees.

gewusst: Sloths can turn their heads very far and so watch their surroundings without moving their bodies.
A long time ago, giant sloths lived in the Americas that could grow as big as an elephant.

teile.einleitung: Where a river flows into the sea or a lake, a delta or a funnel-shaped estuary can form. A delta grows out into the water through deposited material. A funnel-shaped estuary, by contrast, opens out wide towards the sea.
